findings.what: The 'friend who plans everything vs the friend who just shows up' travel meme, also posted as 'Type A friend / Type B friend' and 'Every trip has two friends'. One frame shows two opposite travellers side by side. It holds attention because the viewer picks a side in the first second and then says which one they are in the comments. No setup is needed.
findings.evidence: Searches 'type A friend type B friend travel trend 2026' and 'the friend who plans everything vs just vibes friend'. They returned TikTok discover pages titled 'Friend Who Plans the Whole Trip vs Friend Who Just Asks Who to Venmo', 'Every Trip Has Two Friends That' and 'My Friend Planning The Trip Vs Me', updated between two weeks and a few months before 15 Nov 2026. A 2025 Search Engine Journal roundup cites Hilton's version (tidy suitcase vs forgot her toothbrush). Press coverage from Sept 2025 confirms it as a continuing meme. No origin date and no view counts were found; it is a standing format, not a November spike.
findings.how_for_us: The series already is this meme, so say it in the meme's own words. Shot 1 is the 'two types' picture: Timo's tiny backpack close to camera, Big Yellow filling the middle, Luna's hand on it. Keep that contrast readable at thumbnail size and use it as the cover frame. Post text stays 'Plan or No Plan: which one are you?', and pin the same question as the first comment. Every later episode should have one such side-by-side frame.
findings.risk: Saturated: hotels and airlines have done it since 2025. The press notes these videos often show real resentment between friends, which the bible forbids. Do not use the labels 'Type A / Type B' (American pop psychology, and it has to be read).

findings.what: A situation line in on-screen text from the first frame: 'When your friend ...', 'POV: ...', 'Me vs my friend who ...', 'Types of ...'. It holds attention because most people start with the sound off and the line tells them what they are watching before anything happens.
findings.evidence: Searches 'TikTok hook formats 2026 POV text hook' and 'ppl.studio viral formats November 2026'. ppl.studio (Nov 2026) advises the hook in on-screen text from frame one because most viewers watch muted. Vendor blogs claim POV hooks retain 32 to 42 percent, with no method given. Tryvolume's travel page (measured 8 Nov 2026) lists a 'POV: Trying a Balkan restaurant run by one man' hook at 61 times that account's usual reach. Postdom's scan for 26 Oct to 1 Nov 2026 marks 'POV' as peaking, meaning heavily used. That 'POV' is mocked when the camera is not someone's viewpoint is my own knowledge.
findings.how_for_us: One line, top of frame, in the caption typeface, for the first 1.8 seconds of shot 1 only: 'When your friend packs for one night'. It is gone before Timo's caption 'Luna. It's one night!' appears at about 2.3 seconds, so there are never two texts at once. If a POV line is wanted, the only correct one is 'POV: you travel with these two', because the bible's camera is a third friend. Skip 'Me vs my friend who' (the account is not a person) and 'Types of' (a list of labelled beats that must be read).
findings.risk: The bible's rule 9 says no header; the brief allows one optional line at the top. This needs a decision, and the cut must still pass the silent gate with the line covered. A line longer than seven words, or a second line, brings back the reading problem that sank the first series.

findings.what: Result-first opening: show the finished or most striking moment in the first second, then go back and tell how it happened. It holds attention because the viewer has already seen the reward and stays to learn how they got there.
findings.evidence: Search 'tryvolume what's working TikTok trends this week November 2026'. Tryvolume's pages (measured 8 Nov 2026, self-reported) put this pattern top in three niches: food 'Show the finished bite before any prep' (51 accounts, median 14 times their usual reach), beauty 'Finished look shown first' (41 accounts, 19 times), fitness 'Before-and-after flash in the first seconds' (24 accounts, 16 times). No travel or football figure was found for it.
findings.how_for_us: Make one test version of the pilot that opens with 0.8 seconds of shot 4 (both on the suitcase flying at the camera, Timo screaming), then hard cuts to shot 1 at the station and plays in order. Ship it only if a silent-gate viewer still retells the story correctly; otherwise ship the in-order cut and use the shot 4 frame as the cover image.
findings.risk: A flash-forward is exactly the kind of thing that made the client say he did not understand the plot. It breaks bible rule 5 (cause and effect in order) and shows the ride twice, which weakens the 'No' cut.

findings.what: The refusal smash cut: a character says no, and one hard cut later is doing it (known in film comedy as the Gilligan cut), with the music dropping out on the 'no' and the full beat landing on the cut. It holds attention because the silence makes the viewer wait for the cut.
findings.evidence: Search 'TikTok Gilligan cut smash cut I'm not doing that trend 2026'. It found no named 2026 trend, only TV Tropes and a TikTok discover page 'I'm Not Doing That' (updated 31 Aug 2026) about unrelated character edits. So this is a timeless device, not a trend. Search 'TikTok transitions edit trends autumn 2026' showed cuts snapped to the beat are still the core of CapCut templates ('Beat Edit', 'Velocity Edit 2.0' in mid-2026, per template blogs). Blue Bear Creative's Sept 2026 roundup describes a 'No no no no... Yes' audio trend with the same dislike-then-love flip.
findings.how_for_us: Shot 3 to 4: after Timo's last 'no', hold 6 to 8 frames with only the tick-tock and one wheel squeak, then cut so the full groove and his scream land on the first frame of the ride. Use the same gap length and the same drop in every episode, so the sound alone says 'Plan, No Plan'. In shot 5 let his scream turn into a shouted 'Yes!' as natural sound with no caption: the film then reads as No, then Yes.
findings.risk: Speed ramps, shake or flash effects on the cut would expose faults in generated clips and look like a template. Keep it a plain hard cut. If the gap is longer than about a third of a second, it reads as a mistake.

findings.what: Hold one thing back until the last seconds. The film ends on a small reveal, and the series keeps one question open across episodes. It holds attention because leaving early means missing the answer, and an open question gives people something to write in the comments.
findings.evidence: Search 'tryvolume travel TikTok trends November 2026': 'Place name held back until the last seconds' was used by 15 travel accounts at a median 7 times their usual reach (measured 8 Nov 2026, self-reported). Search 'brands episodic series TikTok 2026': TikTok launched branded mini dramas on 29 June 2026; its showcase series 'Screen Time' ran 57 episodes with a company-reported 560 million views; trade guides call the end of each episode the strongest lever for bringing viewers back.
findings.how_for_us: The pilot already ends on a reveal: 'Timo. This is the small one.' Keep it as the very last second before the card and never put it in the post text. The series question is what is inside Big Yellow: the pinned comment on every episode can ask 'What is in the suitcase?'. This gives a reason to follow without a cliffhanger, so each film still stands alone.
findings.risk: If the suitcase question runs for many episodes with no answer, it turns into the kind of running gag that needs earlier films. The last line is spoken, so with the sound off it works only through the caption.

findings.what: The reaction close-up: a still, silent face holding one clear feeling for two or three seconds, often with one line of text on it. It holds attention because a face is read instantly, and people reuse the clip as their own reaction.
findings.evidence: Search 'ppl.studio viral formats TikTok November 2026': it lists a 'silent face caption trend' among its fastest climbers (viral for 14 creators, top post 74.5 million views, suggested length 23 seconds; self-reported). Postdom's scan for 26 Oct to 1 Nov 2026 marks 'Reaction' as rising. SocialBee's Instagram meme list (11 Nov 2026) is led by two animal reaction images, a nervous Stuart Little and a sad raccoon. That reaction clips and unimpressed cats last for years is my own knowledge.
findings.how_for_us: The pilot has two ready-made ones. Shot 2: Timo's cheek squashed flat on the yellow shell while only his eyes follow the cat. Shot 6: the cat's ears blown flat and its eyes going huge. Compose both so they survive a square crop with nothing else in frame. Post each later as a 5-second loop with one line, for example 'When the cat is faster than you'.
findings.risk: Cutting the cheek-squash moment out of its story could make Timo look like the fool, which the bible forbids, so the line must be about the situation and not about him. The named 'silent face caption' trend will fade within weeks; the reaction clip itself will not.

findings.what: The seamless loop: the last picture matches the first, so the video restarts before the viewer decides to leave. It holds attention through repeat views.
findings.evidence: Search 'TikTok seamless loop 2026 rewatch completion rate'. Several 2026 algorithm guides name rewatch and completion as the heaviest ranking signals, but they are marketing blogs, their thresholds contradict each other (40, 60 and 70 percent completion), and no TikTok document was found. Treat this as widely repeated advice, not as data.
findings.how_for_us: Shot 7 is framed like shot 1 (Luna left, Big Yellow centre, Timo right), which is the right raw material. The weak point is the 2-second cream card between them: a still card is the clearest cue to swipe. Keep the card at 2 seconds or less, let Luna's laugh run under it, and time the five claps so the last dry clap lands on the cut back to frame one, where the suitcase bumps to a stop.
findings.risk: A shorter card gives the brand less time on screen. The loop only works if the first second also makes sense to someone arriving cold.

findings.what: The recurring-character series as a format in its own right. In 2026 viewers follow short episodic shows with the same faces, and TikTok built a product around it. It holds attention across videos: people return for characters they know.
findings.evidence: Searches 'brands episodic series TikTok 2026' and 'AI animated series TikTok 2026'. TikTok launched branded mini dramas on 29 June 2026 (Campaign, eMarketer, MediaPost). YPulse: 56 percent of 13 to 39 year olds want brands to make microseries. On the AI side, 'Fruit Love Island', an AI-generated fruit microdrama, drew very large view counts (a 300 million figure is unverified), then TikTok removed episodes and the creator stopped on 28 March 2026. A viral AI animation in late Sept 2026 was accused of stolen character designs (Creative Bloq).
findings.how_for_us: Make the series recognisable in one second without numbers: the same cover composition for every episode (Luna left, Timo right, the big object between them), the tick-tock from frame one, a TikTok playlist named 'Plan, No Plan', and the same account line. Keep the AI label on every post as the bible says.
findings.risk: AI-made character series are being taken down and criticised this year. Anything that looks like a known studio's characters, or like template AI content, puts the account at risk. Mini drama episodes run 60 to 90 seconds with cliffhangers; do not copy that length or structure.

findings.what: The 'Ba Ba Ba Dance': two people side by side, each does a short solo, then they finish in sync on a 'ba ba ba' hook. It holds attention through the wait for the moment both lock together.
findings.evidence: Searches 'viralremix TikTok trends November 13 2026' and 'Ba Ba Ba dance TikTok trend November 2026'. Viralremix's chart of 13 Nov 2026 ranks it first for new videos, about 42,300 a day, marked at peak and down 6 percent. One blog counts 26,440 videos and 378.7 million views on #bababa on 5 Nov 2026 and credits @otr.j5, 2 Oct 2026. The sound is listed as 'original sound' but is reported to be a remix of 'Don't You Worry 'Bout a Thing' (the 2016 'Sing' film version of a Stevie Wonder song).
findings.how_for_us: Not in the pilot. The useful part is the shape: solo, solo, together. That is already the music theme: Timo's tick on the beat, Luna's cowbell a little late, then both on the five claps. In shot 7, let Timo pat the suitcase lid on the beat, Luna pat it late, and both land the last clap together.
findings.risk: It is at its peak today and will be old by the time a generated, gated film is posted. The sound is an uncleared remix of a famous song. Continuous dance is what generated video does worst. AI tool sites already sell 'Ba Ba Ba from two photos', so an animated version looks like template AI content.

findings.what: 'The Last Dance' trend: two animated characters do a short coordinated routine, spinning hand in hand, to a 2014 Vocaloid track by Maretu. It is the one current trend made mainly by animators with a pair of characters. It holds attention because fans read the pair's relationship in one shared move.
findings.evidence: Search 'The Last Dance trend TikTok 2026 Vocaloid Know Your Meme'. Know Your Meme published its entry on 2 Nov 2026: earliest known animation 14 Aug 2026 (@fugashizzz._, about 529,000 views); the stage-background template by @amy_yayxd on 28 or 29 Aug 2026 had 6.8 million views by 3 Nov; live-action cosplay versions followed in Oct 2026.
findings.how_for_us: Do not make this trend. Take the lesson: a pair of animated characters spreads when they own one synchronised move. Ours is the stand clap (clap, clap, clap-clap-clap), Timo exact and Luna a hair late until the last clap. Show it once per film, hands and faces only, about 2 seconds, never as a dance.
findings.risk: The trend is used for character pairs that fans see as couples, and it is elegant and emotional; both clash with 'friends, never a couple'. The music belongs to someone else. The audience is anime fandom, not football fans.

findings.what: The 'Shoulder Carry' trend: two photos, one person on the other's shoulders, then a flip of who carries whom on the lyric 'cause I'm the one'. The reusable part is the structure: two still pictures and one swap exactly on a sound cue. It holds attention because the second picture arrives on the beat and reverses the first.
findings.evidence: Searches 'viralremix TikTok trends November 13 2026' and 'Shoulder Carry trend TikTok 2026 explained'. Viralremix (13 Nov 2026): about 14,800 new videos a day, down 20 percent, marked past its peak. TikTok discover pages describe it as a couples trend; creators such as ZHC and Brooke Monk are named. The same chart marks 'Bicep Heart' (started end of Oct 2026 per Know Your Meme) and 'AI Baby Dance' as past peak too.
findings.how_for_us: Not the trend, the structure, for a teaser made from two designed start pictures with no video generation. Picture one: the pilot's first frame at the station, Timo pointing, Big Yellow in the way. On the first clap of the theme, picture two: both sitting on Big Yellow mid-ride, arms up. Two pictures, about 6 seconds.
findings.risk: The trend itself is falling and is tagged as a couples trend. It also needs the 'I'm the one' sound, which a brand account cannot use. Two stills with no motion can look cheap next to the film.

findings.what: Split-screen contrast trends: 'It's cool to do both' (two halves show two sides people think cannot go together) and 'Yes... But' (top half the appeal, bottom half the catch). They hold attention because the comparison is read at a glance.
findings.evidence: Searches 'socialbee latest Instagram trends November 11 2026' and 'Yes But split-screen trend October 2026'. SocialBee's Instagram trend page of 11 Nov 2026 describes 'It's cool to do both' (fitness and fast food, dressing up and staying home). The same site covered 'Yes... But' on 7 Oct 2026, and Blue Bear Creative covered a 'Yes But' split-screen in Sept 2026. No sound name or view counts were found.
findings.how_for_us: A later 8-second extra, not the pilot. Top half: Timo's way (his tiny backpack set down neatly, yellow watch beside it). Bottom half: Luna's way (Big Yellow, with the cat sitting on it). Then one full-frame shot of both things side by side with the two friends laughing behind them. 'It's cool to do both' is the bible's tone exactly: each friend is right in turn.
findings.risk: A split screen halves the size of the figures and normally needs labels, which the bible bans. These are Instagram trends dated Sept to Nov 2026 and will read as old within weeks under those names. The side-by-side comparison itself keeps coming back.

top3: One line of text on the first frame, in the meme's own words: 'When your friend packs for one night', top of frame, for the first 1.8 seconds only and gone before Timo's first caption. Post text and pinned comment: 'Plan or No Plan: which one are you?'. It needs no new footage and tells a muted viewer the plot at once. It needs a decision, because bible rule 9 forbids a header while the brief allows one line; the cut must still pass the silent gate with the line covered.

Make the 'No' cut the sound signature of the series. In shot 3, after the last 'no', hold 6 to 8 frames of near silence with only the tick-tock, then land the full groove and Timo's scream on the first frame of the ride. Use the same gap and drop in every episode. In shot 5 his scream becomes a shouted, uncaptioned 'Yes!'. Plain hard cut, no speed ramp, no effect.

End on the reveal and loop tight. 'Timo. This is the small one.' is the last second before the card. The card stays at 2 seconds or less with Luna's laugh under it, and the final clap lands on the cut back to frame one. Pin 'What is in the suitcase?' as the standing series question. Test the 0.8-second result-first opening as a second version only, and ship it only if it passes the silent gate.
avoid: Any trending commercial song or 'original sound' remix. Brand accounts are limited to TikTok's Commercial Music Library, and TikTok's licences do not cover reposting to Reels or Shorts (vendor sources; check TikTok's Business Help Center). The Ba Ba Ba sound is reported to be an uncleared remix of a Stevie Wonder song.

Chasing a named dance or pose trend in the pilot. On the 13 Nov 2026 chart, Ba Ba Ba is at peak, and Shoulder Carry, Bicep Heart and AI Baby Dance are past it. Trackers say sound trends fade in 7 to 10 days and formats in 3 to 4 weeks; a generated film with three gates will arrive late.

Trends that read as a couple: Shoulder Carry (tagged as a couples trend), 'My Moon My Man' soft launches, Bicep Heart (a thirst trap), The Last Dance (used for character pairs fans see as couples). The bible says friends, never a couple.

Ironic or news memes with real people: 'Why would I deceive you?' (Elizabeth Holmes clip, Epidemic Sound 13 Nov 2026), the Jensen Huang memes, the Embassy of Finland memes. They need outside context, use real people, and are irony, which the bible bans.
Seasonal and dated trends: Halloween costume carousels (over on 1 Nov), Mariah Carey 'It's Time', Thanksgiving boards (US only), '2026 is the new 2016' (a January 2026 trend).

Prank and contest formats: the 'closing door prank' (took off 28 Oct 2026; someone runs into a shutting door) and the rock-paper-scissors food challenge. The first is humiliation; the second needs precise hands and fast eating, which generated video does badly.

Text-heavy formats: 'Types of ...' lists, 'Tell me you're X without telling me', 'We listen and we don't judge', 'This is your sign'. They must be read, which is what the client rejected. One line at most.

Looking like template AI content: Italian brainrot styles, 'from two photos' AI trend templates, anything close to a known studio's characters. 'Fruit Love Island' had episodes removed by TikTok and a Sept 2026 AI animation was accused of stolen designs.
Slang and trend words in captions. In a small 2026 poll (92 Gen Z respondents, dcdx) 85 percent called brands saying 'bestie' cringe. 'POV:' is wrong unless the camera really is someone's viewpoint.
Speed ramps, velocity edits, morph or zoom transitions laid over generated clips. They show faults and fail the fault gate. Use plain hard cuts on the beat.

Counting on photo carousels for reach. Buffer's 2026 data puts TikTok video at 3.39 percent median engagement against 1.92 percent for carousels, and Metricool reports carousel views down 23 percent in early 2026.
search_note:
I ran 42 web searches on 15 Nov 2026. I could not open any page: the two fetches I tried (virlo.ai, newengen.com) did not resolve, and both hosts would have to be allowed in the session's network settings. Everything here comes from search-result summaries, not from the pages or the apps.

Reliability is moderate to low for named trends. Most sources are trend trackers, tool vendors and SEO blogs with self-reported numbers and no method, and their rankings disagree. Some recycle old trends: one lists 'We listen and we don't judge' (late 2024) as peaking, another lists 'Suspect' as an October trend. The best-dated sources are Know Your Meme (entries of early Nov 2026), the Viralremix chart of 13 Nov 2026, Tryvolume's pages measured 8 Nov 2026, SocialBee's pages of 11 Nov 2026 and Epidemic Sound's article of 13 Nov 2026.

I found no named, current format specific to football trips, and no evidence that the refusal smash cut is a trend; those points and the notes on 'POV' misuse and reaction clips are my own knowledge. The loop and completion-rate figures are unverified. Before posting, someone should check TikTok's Creative Center in the app on the day.

findings.what: What 'trendy, fun music' sounds like on TikTok in autumn 2026: club-derived, drum-and-bassline-led dance music with a bounce, bright or major, roughly 120 to 135 BPM, with tiny chopped vocal hooks. Not guitar pop, not lo-fi, not 'cinematic'. Four live flavours: (a) afro house, about 118-125 BPM: shakers, congas, round or log-drum bass, pumping pads; (b) UK garage and speed garage, about 130-138 BPM: swung 2-step hats, organ bass, pitched one-syllable vocal chops; (c) Brazilian funk 'montagem', about 130 BPM: tamborzao hand percussion, chopped shouts; (d) glossy Latin and electro dance-pop. Comedy sketches themselves mostly run on their own original audio (dialogue plus a light bed), not on a song.
findings.evidence: Searches run 15 Nov 2026, result summaries only. Splice x MIDiA 'Sounds of 2026' (Jan 2026): afro house named Sound of the Year, sample downloads +778%; speed garage +625%. TikTok newsroom (1-2 Sep 2026): UK Song of the Summer 2026 is Kyla and DJ Paleface 'Do You Mind' (2008), Silva Bumpa 'On 2nite' at no. 3, a Prospa and Cloonee track in the top 10; UK #UKGarage posts +42% and #HouseMusic +53% Feb-Jul 2026. Tokchart (third-party tracker): October 2026 top three were 'BbY WOW' (Karol G, Judeline, rusowsky), 'Nicole Kidman' (ADELA, about 3.4M posts, described as unapologetic electropop) and 'Runaway' (AURORA); fastest growing on 7 Nov 2026 were 'Paper Moon Static', 'Halloween Party' and 'Montagem da Chupeta' (Brazilian funk). Billboard Brasil: #brazilianphonk posts in Europe +62% Feb-May 2026. SocialPilot's list for 27 Oct-5 Nov 2026 is led by plain 'original sound' entries. The BPM ranges and instrument lists are my own knowledge.
findings.how_for_us: The bible's theme (afro house with an amapiano log drum at 120 BPM) is already inside the trend at genre level, so keep it; it is not a retro or stock choice. What it lacks are the 'right now' markers: a pitched one-syllable vocal chop answering the claps, a pumping organ stab, a dry room sound. Uphill (shot 2) the lazy log drum alone carries the joke; the ride (shots 4-5) is where the full club groove plays. Generate a UK-garage challenger (brief B) and compare both on a phone with three people aged 18 to 25.
findings.risk: Genre fashion moves. UK garage is a UK-centred wave; afro house was crowned in January 2026 and may feel like last year by mid 2027. A series theme cannot change monthly, so pick a groove, not a gimmick. Chart data is from a third-party tracker whose own pages disagree on counts.

findings.what: Old songs are winning, so 'trendy' also means 'familiar on first listen'. The biggest TikTok songs of 2026 are catalogue tracks from 2008 to 2016, and nostalgic, warm, big-chorus music sits under friend and travel montages. The usable lesson for an original track: a two- or three-note hook in a major key, simple enough to hum after one viewing, with some 2008-2016 warmth (round organ bass, a gang chorus).
findings.evidence: TikTok newsroom and Music Business Worldwide (1 Sep 2026): global and US Song of the Summer 2026 is Katy Perry 'The One That Got Away' (2011); the whole US top four is catalogue; Mac Miller 'Cinderella' (2016) is no. 1 in Canada; UK no. 1 is from 2008; Oasis 'Champagne Supernova' entered the UK list through 'fan content, football videos and cultural nostalgia'. Zara Larsson's 'Lush Life' (2015) revival: over 14.5 billion views, searches for '2016' on TikTok +452% in the first week of 2026. Roisin Murphy 'Ramalama (Bang Bang)' (2005) back for costume walks, about 525,000 videos (Tokchart). Travel-audio roundups from June to September 2026 list Robyn 'Dancing On My Own', Sade 'Kiss of Life' and a warm 'Mediterranean' instrumental for trip recaps.
findings.how_for_us: Judge the 'oh-oh-oh' plus the five-clap pattern by one test: play the pilot once, and ten minutes later ask the viewer to hum or clap the hook. If they cannot, simplify it. Put a warm round organ note under the hook on the payoff (shot 7) so the hug lands with a feeling of memory, not only energy.
findings.risk: A nostalgic pastiche can drift close to a real song; a generator can do this by accident. Run the finished master through a song-recognition app and ask two football fans whether the hook reminds them of a real chant ('Ole ole', 'Seven Nation Army', 'Freed from Desire' must not be heard in it). 'Familiar' can also slide into 'generic'.

findings.what: The rule: a brand cannot put a trending commercial song under its video, on any of the three platforms. TikTok: a business account's sound picker shows only 'Commercial Sounds' (the Commercial Music Library, reported as 1M+ pre-cleared tracks with almost no major-label hits); the general library is licensed for personal, non-commercial use, and content promoting a brand counts as commercial even from a personal or creator account. The CML licence covers TikTok only. Instagram: business accounts get Meta's royalty-free Sound Collection (about 14,000 tracks) instead of the licensed catalogue; the 'Original audio' label on someone else's Reel is not a licence. YouTube Shorts: the Shorts library is for personal, non-commercial use unless you hold the licences. Sped-up versions, covers, 'only five seconds' and 'credit in the caption' change nothing.
findings.evidence: Searches on TikTok CML rules, Instagram business music rules and YouTube Shorts rules: mostly vendor blogs (Soundstripe, Foxi Music, Dynamoi), consistent on the core rule, conflicting on details; I could not open TikTok's or Meta's own help pages. Lawsuit search: Warner v. Crumbl (April 2025, 159 songs in TikTok and Instagram posts, 23.85M dollars claimed); Sony v. DSW (6 Aug 2025, 200+ songs, influencer posts included); major labels and publishers v. Quince (April 2026, 130+ works, plus liability for influencers' posts). Music Week reports a rights-recovery firm scanning 350,000+ TikTok posts from 1,000+ brands in 18 months. Not legal advice.
findings.how_for_us: One owned, original master is mixed into the film file and the same file goes to TikTok, Reels and Shorts. The sentence for the founder: 'Trendy means it sounds like this month's feed; it cannot be this month's hit, because labels are suing brands for exactly that, and an own sound is what can become our trend.' The scarf seller, the stadium and any radio in a scene never play a real song either.
findings.risk: The founder may still hear 'trendy' as 'the song I know'. If he insists, the only legal routes are a paid sync and master licence or a track from the platform's commercial library, chosen separately per platform. Terms change; check the live account before posting.

findings.what: The workaround creators use, and its limits for a brand. (1) Post with your own track baked in: the upload becomes 'original sound' under the account; a business account is shown a 'Music Usage Confirmation' box to tick, stating it holds the rights. (2) Add a licensed sound inside the app at posting time: for a brand this means only a Commercial Music Library track on TikTok (TikTok Creative Center lets you filter songs by 'Approved for business use') or a Sound Collection track on Instagram. (3) The 'hidden sound' trick: attach a trending sound at 1-3% volume under your own audio to appear on its sound page. Instagram also has 'Replace Audio' (launched about 22 July 2026): swap the in-app music on a published post without losing engagement.
findings.evidence: Searches: 'Music Usage Confirmation' (vendor blogs agree on the tick box; they conflict on whether a business account can import its own audio as a reusable original sound); 'trending sound at zero volume' (one vendor source describes the 1-3% tactic, no independent test that it helps reach); 'Instagram replace audio' (Music Business Worldwide and others, July 2026; coverage of Reels disputed). I also checked the read-only tool in this workspace that lists trending Commercial Music Library tracks: no TikTok account is connected, so I could not pull the live chart; per its description it attaches music only on direct posts, not drafts.
findings.how_for_us: Use route 1 for every film. Before the pilot goes out, upload a private test from the real Venuvoy account with the real master to see exactly what the app asks and whether the sound can be reused by others. Keep route 2 only as a TikTok-only experiment on a repost, never on the main cut, because an in-app track replaces our theme and breaks the beat-synced edit. Do not use route 3: for a brand it is legal only with library tracks, unproven, and it gives the sound credit to someone else's track.
findings.risk: Ticking the confirmation box creates no rights; it only records our statement. A TikTok export that contains a library track must never be cross-posted to Reels or Shorts. Menus and account types differ by country and change often.

findings.what: Original music from a text-to-music model: what we actually have and the rules around it. Listed in this workspace: ElevenLabs Music v2 and v2.5 (text prompt or custom lyrics, 3 to 600 seconds, a 'force instrumental' switch, up to four variations per request) and a stem-separation tool. The listed sound-effect model is marked 'game pipeline only', so confirm the sound-effect route before planning on it. ElevenLabs states its music model is trained on licensed material and that paid plans carry commercial rights; free-tier output is not cleared. Platform rules: no AI vocal that imitates a real person's voice; realistic AI audio and video must be labelled.
findings.evidence: Read-only model list in this workspace (15 Nov 2026). Search 'ElevenLabs Music commercial use 2026': model terms pages dated 26 May and 9 Oct 2026 in the results; sources agree paid plans allow commercial use and conflict on advertising at lower tiers. Search on TikTok AI rules: third-party reports of a January 2026 ban on AI vocals built from a real voice, mandatory AI disclosure in ads from 21 July 2026, 3 billion+ items labelled by July 2026 with automatic C2PA detection. Search on AI music ownership: purely AI-generated music may not get copyright protection.
findings.how_for_us: Generate four variations of one 64-second master per brief, choose on a phone speaker, then lock ONE master for the whole series and never regenerate per film (changing voices sank the first series; changing music would do the same). Split it into stems so the edit can drop layers as the bible wants. For the wordless hook, leave 'force instrumental' off and, if the model invents words, use custom lyrics containing only 'Oh, oh, oh' and 'Hey', or generate the chant and claps as a separate a cappella stem in the same key and tempo. Never type an artist or song name into the prompt. Keep the prompt, date, job number and plan receipt as proof of rights.
findings.risk: Our rights come through the platform we generate on, so its plan terms must allow commercial use. Weak copyright in AI music means we can use it but may not be able to stop copies. A generated track can accidentally resemble a real one. Vocals in generated music are the least controllable part.

findings.what: How to ask for the music so it sounds current and not like stock or advert music. Stock gives itself away by: a slow intro, ukulele, whistling, glockenspiel, bright piano chords, strummed guitar with stomps and 'hey' shouts, a riser into a cymbal crash, a wide polished mix, a fade-out. Current tracks: start on the groove in the first half second; drums and bass lead; one hook of two or three notes; a pitched one-syllable vocal chop; chords that pump with the kick; percussion that lands slightly late; dry, close, slightly crunchy sound; real claps in a room; a dead stop instead of a riser; an abrupt dry ending. Describe it to the model as a club record, never with the words background, upbeat, happy, uplifting, corporate, inspiring, advert or jingle, which pull it towards stock.
findings.evidence: My own production knowledge, not a search result. Supported indirectly by the genre evidence in finding 1 and by the series music note, which already bans whistling, ukulele, trailer drums and whoosh effects. The 'stomp, clap, hey' sound was widely mocked online in 2025 (my own knowledge).
findings.how_for_us: Every brief names tempo, key, instruments, the order of sections with seconds, the hook, and a list of things to leave out. Ask for a 64-second track with sections of at least four bars so the editor can lift clean two-bar blocks. Ask for a log drum or bass 'with a clear mid-range knock that carries on a phone speaker'. Choose between variations on a phone speaker at half volume, never on headphones.
findings.risk: The series' own five-clap pattern and gang 'oh-oh-oh' sit one step from the mocked stomp-clap-hey advert sound. They stay cool only over club drums, sung rough and slightly flat by a few voices, short, with no acoustic guitar and no floor stomp.

findings.what: STYLE BRIEF A, 'Tick Tock Clap' (keeps the bible; recommended). Paste-ready: 'A sunny afro house club track with an amapiano log-drum bounce. Exactly 120 BPM, 4/4, F major. No intro and no fade: it starts on beat one with a tidy woodblock and muted marimba tick-tock exactly on the beat and a tight shaker. After 8 seconds a lazy, knocky log-drum bassline joins, with a clear mid-range knock that carries on a phone speaker, and a cowbell that lands a little late. After 16 seconds it thins to bass and shaker for 8 seconds, then one beat of total silence. Then the drop: a soft round four-on-the-floor kick, congas and shekere, off-beat open hi-hat, the log drum, warm organ stabs that pump with the kick, a short pitched-up one-syllable vocal chop answering every second bar, real group handclaps in a room playing clap, clap, clap-clap-clap, and four young friends, mixed voices, singing a rough, slightly out-of-tune three-note oh-oh-oh with no words. After 16 seconds of full groove, a 6-second breakdown of shaker and tick-tock only, then the full groove and the oh-oh-oh return and it ends on three dry handclaps with no reverb tail. Dry, close, hand-played, slightly imperfect timing; drums and percussion lead. No lyrics, no guitar, no piano, no ukulele, no whistling, no glockenspiel, no risers, no whoosh, no cinematic drums, no supersaw synth.' Length 64 seconds, vocals allowed, four variations.
findings.evidence: Built from the series bible and music note (120 BPM, two motifs, five claps, three-note chant) plus the genre evidence: afro house was Splice and MIDiA's Sound of the Year for 2026 (+778% downloads). The added markers (vocal chop, pumping organ, dead stop before the drop) are my own knowledge of the genre.
findings.how_for_us: Fits the pilot without re-timing: at 120 BPM every half second is one beat. Tick-tock alone under 'Luna. It's one night!'; the log drum enters with the uphill push; the dead stop is the 'No'; the drop is the hard cut onto the suitcase ride; the chant enters on Timo's laugh; the breakdown is the cat; the three dry claps are the end card.
findings.risk: The amapiano log drum has been everywhere since 2021 and can sound a year old to listeners in South Africa or the UK. If the log drum has no mid-range knock it vanishes on a phone and the theme turns into shaker and claps, which reads as advert music.

findings.what: STYLE BRIEF B, 'Sunny 2-Step' (the challenger; the most 2026 for UK and European feeds). Paste-ready: 'A sunny, cheeky UK garage club track with a speed-garage bounce. Exactly 130 BPM, 4/4, G major. No intro and no fade: it starts on beat one with a woodblock tick-tock on the beat and shuffled closed hi-hats. After 7 seconds a swung 2-step drum pattern joins (kick on one plus a late skipping kick, crisp rimshot on two and four) with a warm, round, bouncy two-bar organ bass riff that is clearly audible on a phone speaker, bright filtered chord stabs, and chopped, pitched-up one-syllable female vocal slices used as rhythm, no words. After 15 seconds it thins to bass and hats, then one beat of total silence. Then the drop: the full 2-step groove with a deeper bass, real group handclaps in a room playing clap, clap, clap-clap-clap, and four young friends singing a rough three-note oh-oh-oh with no words. A short breakdown of hats and tick-tock, then the full groove returns and it ends on three dry handclaps with no reverb tail. Dry, punchy, swung, warm, slightly crunchy like an old sampler. No MC, no rap, no lyrics, no sirens, no air horn, no dark reese bass, no dubstep wobble, no rave stabs, no piano house chords, no risers.' Length 64 seconds, vocals allowed, four variations.
findings.evidence: TikTok newsroom, 2 Sep 2026: 'UK garage takes over the summer', UK no. 1 'Do You Mind', Silva Bumpa 'On 2nite' at no. 3, #UKGarage posts +42% Feb-Jul 2026. Splice and MIDiA (Jan 2026): speed garage +625%. The drum, bass and vocal-chop description is my own knowledge of the genre.
findings.how_for_us: Gives Luna's side of the story a skippy, teasing bounce and makes the ride feel faster. Keep the same beat counts per shot as now (8, 8, 9, 5, 5, 6, 11, and 4 for the card): at 130 BPM the film then runs about 25.9 seconds instead of 28, each shot about 8% shorter (4.0 seconds becomes 3.7).
findings.risk: Leaves the 120 BPM grid on which the scripts were timed: the card drops to 1.85 seconds (give it 5 beats) and the last shot's two spoken lines get tight (give it 13 beats). Strongly UK-coded; viewers elsewhere may not read it as 'the current sound'. Done badly it turns dark and clubby, which fights the warm tone.

findings.what: STYLE BRIEF C, 'Matchday Baile' (the loud option, closest to football-edit energy). Paste-ready: 'A bright, sunny Brazilian funk and street-drum track. Exactly 130 BPM, 4/4, major key. No intro and no fade: it starts on beat one with a woodblock tick-tock and a tamborim pattern. After 7 seconds the tamborzao funk rhythm joins, played on real hand drums: low surdo, pandeiro, and agogo bells that land a little late, with a short punchy kick and a simple two-note bounce bass that carries on a phone speaker, and staccato one-syllable shout hits used as rhythm, no words. After 15 seconds it thins to bass and shaker, then one beat of total silence. Then the drop: the full drum corps, real group handclaps playing clap, clap, clap-clap-clap, and a small group of young friends singing a rough three-note oh-oh-oh with no words. A short breakdown of shaker and tick-tock, then the full groove returns and it ends on three dry handclaps. Daylight, playful, a street party outside a stadium. No words in any language, no distorted cowbell melody, no drift phonk, no dark or aggressive mood, no sirens, no gunshots, no heavy distortion, no whistles, no brass fanfare, no risers.' Length 64 seconds, vocals allowed, four variations.
findings.evidence: Tokchart, 7 Nov 2026: 'Montagem da Chupeta' among the three fastest-growing sounds worldwide. Billboard Brasil: #brazilianphonk posts in Europe +62% Feb-May 2026; 'Montagem Xonada' used in 1.7M+ videos. World Cup 2026 content passed 1.2 trillion views on TikTok (TikTok newsroom, July 2026), so drum-led football sound is fresh in this audience's ears. Rhythm and instrument details are my own knowledge.
findings.how_for_us: Luna's late cowbell becomes late agogo bells and the stadium drums in the natural sound can be the same drum corps, so the theme seems to come from the ground the friends are walking towards. Same beat counts and the same 130 BPM re-timing as brief B.
findings.risk: Codes as one country, against the bible's invented town and 'nothing of one country'. The football-edit version of this sound is dark and aggressive; the wrong generation will sound like a gym or car edit. Individual montagem flavours turn over in weeks. Highest chance of sounding like 'world music' stock.

findings.what: Cutting to the beat. On TikTok the standard grammar is: cuts land on beats, the big reveal lands on the drop, and the drop is set up by a moment of nothing. The series' signature (a 'No', then a hard cut to both doing it) is exactly that device, but the current timing puts the drop on the wrong beat. At 120 BPM a beat is 0.5 seconds; shots 1 to 3 last 4 + 4 + 4.5 = 12.5 seconds = 25 beats, so the hard cut falls on beat two of bar seven if the music simply runs from frame one; shot 5 starts five beats after the cut, so the chant would also enter off the downbeat.
findings.evidence: Search 'TikTok editing trends 2026 beat sync': vendor guides (Opus, May 2026; CapCut 2026; Splice app, 10 March 2026) agree that mapping cuts to beats, drops and audio cues is still the core technique and that auto beat-sync templates are standard; nothing specific on comedy timing. The arithmetic is mine, from the shot lengths in the pilot script; the fix is my own editing knowledge.
findings.how_for_us: (1) Build for exactly six bars, 0 to 12.0 s. (2) From 12.0 to 12.5 s the music stops dead: only the tick-tock, the outdoor air and Timo's last 'no'. The two hollow pats on the lid sit on the last two beats before the stop and act as the drum fill. (3) The drop restarts the bar count exactly on the cut at 12.5 s, with Timo's scream starting on that frame in place of a crash. (4) Make shot 4 2.0 s and shot 5 3.0 s (same total): the 'oh-oh-oh' then enters on a downbeat at 14.5 s and the laugh gets the extra half second. (5) Shot 7 starts at 20.5 s, a downbeat, so the hook returns on the hug. (6) Card 26.0 to 28.0 s: one beat of breath, the three claps on its last three beats, the final one dry. Optional: in shots 1 and 2 filter the groove as if it leaks from the stadium over the hill and open it at the hilltop when the stadium appears.
findings.risk: Cutting every shot on a bar line makes a film feel like a template; only three points must be exact (the drop, the chant entry, the claps). Lip-synced lines must not be squeezed to fit the grid: move the music edit, not the mouth.

findings.what: How original sounds spread, and how ours could. A sound travels when it is a short, complete unit that other people can act out with their own footage; in 2026 the repeatable format matters more than the song. For this series the unit already exists: the spoken 'No. No, no, no.', one beat of nothing, then the drop with a scream that turns into a laugh, about seven seconds. Anyone can film 'my friend suggests it, I say no, cut, we are doing it' to that audio.
findings.evidence: Search on Jet2holidays: a travel brand's own advert audio became TikTok's global Song of the Summer 2025 (announced 4 Sep 2025; voiceover in 2M+ creations, the song in 9M+ videos, 80 billion views), used over travel mishaps, and took off after the brand joined in in April 2025. Search on Dr Pepper: a creator's improvised jingle posted about 23 Dec 2025 was licensed and aired by the brand on 19 Jan 2026; 65M views reported; 35+ brand accounts then asked for jingles. WERSM article 'TikTok Trends Are Becoming Formats, Not Just Sounds' and SocialPilot (Nov 2026: two sounds doubled in six days because of the format). A how-to source says a TikTok original sound can be renamed and disappears if the source video is deleted (single source).
findings.how_for_us: Make those seven seconds identical in every film: the same two bars of music, the 'No' in the same place, nothing else spoken over it, whichever friend says it. After the pilot, rename the sound on TikTok and Instagram to something findable such as 'No. No, no, no. (Plan, No Plan)'. Never delete a posted film; set it to private if needed. The post text can stay as the bible has it; do not ask people to use the sound.
findings.risk: Most original sounds are never reused; this must not bend the story. Sources conflict on whether a business account's original sound is freely reusable, so test it on the real account. If the sound does travel, we cannot control what it is used on.

findings.what: Sound effects and the mix for a phone. Current short comedy uses few effects and makes real sounds do the work: crisp close foley, placed on the beat, with the music getting out of the way. Library meme effects (the boom, the record scratch, cartoon boings) read as an older brand trying to be funny. Loudness: start at about -14 LUFS integrated with peaks under -1 dBTP, then judge by ear on a phone.
findings.evidence: Search 'TikTok loudness LUFS 2026': no official figure; -14 LUFS and -1 dBTP is the most repeated, other sources say -16 or -9 to -12, and one warns that TikTok compresses again in the app. Search on editing trends: guides treat a well-timed hit as a retention tool. The rest (meme effects, foley on the grid, phone-speaker bass) is my own knowledge and matches the series note that natural sound is as loud as the music.
findings.how_for_us: Shot 1: the suitcase's heavy bump is the first downbeat. Shot 2: the grinding wheels run in time like a second shaker, the puffing falls on beats, and the cat's 'mrrp' sits in a gap. Shot 3: the two lid pats are the fill before the stop. Shot 4: the scream starts on the drop. Shot 6: the music drops out so the gust and the small 'mrrow' are the joke. Shot 7 and the card: Luna's laugh runs over the last claps, not cut clean. Lower the music about 6 to 9 dB under the three spoken lines. Check the master in mono on a phone speaker at half volume: the bass must still be heard as a knock, and the tick-tock and claps must carry the tune when it is not.
findings.risk: Sounds placed too exactly on the grid turn the film into a music video and the people stop feeling real; keep laughs and breaths loose. The loudness number is not confirmed by TikTok. Any music or voices the video clips generated themselves must be removed, as the series note says.

top3: Own the sound: one original theme mixed into the file, the same master on TikTok, Reels and Shorts, no commercial song in any form, rights receipts kept, and a private test upload from the real account first. Tell the founder plainly that 'trendy' means the sound of this month's feed, because labels are suing brands that borrow this month's hit.

Keep the 120 BPM afro-house theme (brief A) but harden it so it sounds like autumn 2026 and not like stock: starts on the groove in the first half second, a log drum with a mid-range knock that survives a phone speaker, a pitched one-syllable vocal chop, pumping organ, dry room claps, rough gang voices. Generate brief B as the challenger and pick on a phone with three people aged 18 to 25. Lock one master for the whole series and split it into stems.

Put the drop exactly on the hard cut with one beat of dead silence on the 'No' before it (build for six bars to 12.0 s, stop for one beat, drop at 12.5 s; shot 4 at 2.0 s and shot 5 at 3.0 s so the chant enters on a downbeat), and keep that seven-second 'No, silence, drop, scream into laugh' identical in every film so it can become the series' own reusable sound.
avoid: Any commercial trending song under the film (for example 'BbY WOW', 'Nicole Kidman', 'Do You Mind', 'The One That Got Away'), including sped-up versions, remixes, covers, a few seconds only, credit in the caption, or posting from a personal or creator account to get the full library.
Reusing another account's 'original sound' that contains music, and cross-posting a TikTok export that carries a Commercial Music Library track to Reels or Shorts.
The hidden-sound trick (a trending sound at 1-3% volume under our audio): unproven, legal for a brand only with library tracks, and it gives the sound credit away.

Typing an artist or song name, or 'in the style of', into the music generator; any AI vocal that imitates a real voice; any hook that echoes a real chant ('Ole ole', 'Seven Nation Army', 'Freed from Desire', the thunder clap).
An AI 'football anthem' with sung names of players or countries: a summer 2026 World Cup fad, already dated, and it brings in real names the bible forbids.

Stock and advert signals: a slow intro, ukulele, whistling, glockenspiel, bright piano chords, strummed guitar with stomps and 'hey', risers and whooshes, a fade-out, and the prompt words upbeat, happy, corporate, uplifting, background, jingle.
Meme sound effects from a library (boom, record scratch, cartoon boing, sad trombone).
Dark drift phonk, hard techno or aggressive edit music, and lo-fi 'chill beats' or cinematic music: wrong tone in both directions.
Chasing this week's sound or season ('Paper Moon Static', Halloween audio, cosy autumn audio): it will be over before the pilot is posted and the series world is always sunny.
Regenerating the music for each film, or letting the theme, key or tempo drift between films.
Music louder than the laughs, wheels and voices, or judged only on headphones.
Deleting a posted film (it can kill its sound) and asking viewers to 'use this sound'.

findings.what: "Fruit Love Island" by @ai.cinema021, the biggest openly AI-made character series of 2026: a dating-show parody where every contestant is a talking fruit. Daily episodes of 2 to 4 minutes, numbered and given teaser titles (the most watched was "New Dates... New Doubts"), a fixed cast who flirt, argue and confront each other, and viewers who vote in the comments for their favourite couple and for who should leave. Storyline suggestions were taken through a link in the bio. Spanish-language copies ("frutinovelas") run from under a minute to two minutes.
findings.evidence: Searches: "Fruit Love Island episodes views", "Fruit Love Island creator statement mass reporting", "BBC Fruit Love Island fans voting", "frutinovelas". Launched 13 March 2026; about 300 million views in nine days; 3.1 to 3.3 million followers by 23 March; episodes averaged 10 to 15 million views, the top one 39 million (The Decoder, The Star, Tribune, Know Your Meme as summarised). Stopped on 28 March 2026 after mass reporting removed roughly 12 of 22 episodes; reports cited fake engagement and unlabelled AI (The Cool Down, Daily Dot, Gigazine). BBC, 29 March 2026, via secondary reports: fans vote for favourite couple and who leaves. Critics called it "the perfect example of AI slop" and mocked glitches such as mismatched limb colours. All figures are press-reported, not checked on the platform; outlets disagree on the episode count (19 to 28).
findings.how_for_us: Copy the mechanics, not the content. (1) Side-taking: keep the post text "Plan or No Plan: which one are you?" and repeat it as a pinned first comment from the account, then answer early comments as Team Plan or Team No Plan. (2) Launch burst: have three finished films before the pilot is posted and release them inside the first ten days. (3) Let comments choose between two next situations ("next trip: the hostel bunk or the scarf seller?"), in the post text only, never in the film. (4) AI label on from the first post.
findings.risk: Votes and "what happens next" pull towards cliffhangers, which the bible forbids, so the vote must stay outside the film. Part of that audience was hate-watching and the show was reported off the platform within 15 days: reach without goodwill does not last. The fruit and micro-drama look is already tagged as slop, and its cheating plots are the opposite of our tone.

findings.what: The audio tag as character, from "Italian brainrot" (2025): each AI character is one look plus one short chanted sound repeated in every video ("Tung tung tung sahur", "Ballerina Cappuccina, mi mi mi mi"). The chant is the hook in the first second, it is what viewers type in the comments and reuse as a sound, and it let the characters travel between accounts. Comments were about lore: family trees, who is married to whom, who would win.
findings.evidence: Search: "Italian brainrot characters Tung Tung Sahur Ballerina Cappuccina how it grew 2025". Tung Tung Tung Sahur was made in February 2025 by @noxaasht; Ballerina Cappuccina in March 2025, about 19.5 million views in three weeks with her audio; fans built family trees; brands and even Hungary's prime minister posted versions (RTE, September 2025; Malay Mail, August 2025; some dates from low-authority wiki pages). Search: "Dumb Ways to Die TikTok account growth": the 2023 comeback ran on its own jingle, 1.2 billion views of the trend in 30 days and 65,000 template versions (Mumbrella, figures from the owner).
findings.how_for_us: Make the "No" a fixed four-beat sound bite: "No. No, no, no." always in the same rhythm on the 120 beats-a-minute grid, the music drops to the tick-tock alone, and the hard cut lands on the downbeat with the five claps (clap, clap, clap-clap-clap). Identical in every film, whichever friend says it. Publish that four-second stretch as a named original sound ("Plan, No Plan: the No") so viewers can put it over their own "I said no, then did it" clips. In the pilot this is shot 3 into shot 4: Luna's giggle must not cover the last "no".
findings.risk: Brainrot itself is a 2025 trend for children and reads as nonsense, which is exactly what the client rejected: copy only the audio-tag mechanism. A catchphrase that is pushed ("say it with us") is cringe; it should simply recur.

findings.what: How series are titled and numbered. Three patterns exist: plain running numbers (Skibidi Toilet: "skibidi toilet 1, 2, 3...", first episode 11 seconds long), "Episode N" plus a teaser title (Fruit Love Island), and "Part N" for micro-dramas. All three belong to stories that continue. Stand-alone sketch series (Chikn Nuggit) use no numbers: the series name and the characters carry it, and the platform playlist does the linking.
findings.evidence: Searches: "animated shorts series ... Skibidi Toilet episode numbering" (first episode 7 February 2023, 11 seconds; over 65 billion views by November 2023 per a Wikipedia mirror; 77 or more episodes by mid-2026, low-authority source) and "TikTok episodic series best practice 2026" (marketing blogs: label every part, every part must hook on its own, a TikTok playlist name is limited to 25 characters; TikTok Series and a Reels series test exist). The Chikn Nuggit naming pattern is my own knowledge.
findings.how_for_us: Keep the bible's "no numbers". Title every post in one pattern: "Plan, No Plan: One Night" (series name, colon, a two or three word title naming the big object). Create a playlist called "Plan, No Plan" (12 characters) on TikTok and on YouTube Shorts with the pilot, so a viewer who likes one film is served the next. Use the frame-one still as cover, with that film's big object in the centre, so the profile grid reads as a row of bright objects, Big Yellow first.
findings.risk: "Ep. 4" tells a newcomer that three were missed, and a "Part 2" promise breaks the stand-alone rule. A title that needs explaining repeats the failure of the first series.

findings.what: The AI character vlog: a non-human character holds the camera selfie-style and talks to the viewer in plain everyday speech, one main character, one place, clips of about eight seconds, speech from the first frame. It began with Bigfoot, then Yeti as his friend, then stormtroopers and Bible figures.
findings.evidence: Search: "Bigfoot vlog Veo 3 AI character vlog trend format". First @bigfootvlogs video on 25 May 2025, 676,400 likes within a month (Know Your Meme); one Bigfoot account reached 250,000 followers and 35 million views with 20 posts (Kapwing); creators usually name the tool (Veo 3) in the description; their advice is one main character and simple everyday language. Wired reported the same format being used for racist caricatures.
findings.how_for_us: Do not copy the selfie talk (the bible forbids "hey guys"). Copy two things. (1) Speech at once: in the pilot's shot 1 Timo's eyes travel up the suitcase and his arm sinks before he speaks, so the first word comes after about three seconds. Start "Luna. It's one night!" inside the first second and a half, over the bump of the suitcase, and let his eyes travel and his arm sink after the line. (2) The camera is a person: the bible's "third friend filming" should be felt once per film. In shot 3 Luna can throw one quick look into the lens as she pats the lid, as if inviting us to ride too.
findings.risk: The vlog format peaked in summer 2025; a full selfie vlog now would look late. More than one look into the lens per film turns it into a vlog and weakens the two-friends story.

findings.what: The wordless, music-led 3D character that works in every country: Nobody Sausage, a simple brightly coloured figure with no dialogue who moves to music, one move per post, loopable. Related: the official Dumb Ways to Die account, whose clips run under seven seconds on its own jingle.
findings.evidence: Search: "Nobody Sausage 3D animated character TikTok followers brand collaborations". Created in 2020 by Brazilian animator Kael Cabral; about 33 million followers across TikTok, Instagram and X and over 3 billion views (Decrypt and CoinMarketCap, figures from 2024 to 2025, not current); partners named include Hugo Boss, Netflix, Adidas and Ryan Reynolds' Maximum Effort; MIDiA Research published a case study on it. Dumb Ways to Die: clips under seven seconds, 3.4 million TikTok followers by March 2023 (Naavik, Gameshub). What the videos look like is my own knowledge. Search "TikTok business account trending sounds Commercial Music Library 2026": vendor guides say a business account may use only the pre-cleared commercial library or separately licensed music.
findings.how_for_us: Put the action on the beat so the film is clear with the sound off and feels like music with it on. Pilot: Luna's two pats on the lid (shot 3) are the first two claps of the stand pattern; the hard cut to the ride is the downbeat; Timo's fist goes up (shot 5) on the "oh-oh-oh"; his cheek lands on the lid on the last dry clap. Between films, post six to eight second loops cut from them: the cat's fur blown flat as the suitcase streaks past (shot 6) loops cleanly.
findings.risk: Do not make Timo and Luna dance to chart sounds: a brand account cannot use most of them, and dance trends date in weeks. The client's "trendy music" has to come from our own theme sounding current. Loops must be new edits, not reposts, or the channel looks repetitive.

findings.what: The stand-alone cartoon sketch with a tiny one-trait cast: Chikn Nuggit. Each film is one small gag of 15 to 20 seconds, no carry-over, a handful of characters who are each one trait and one colour, and physical comedy before dialogue.
findings.evidence: Search: "Chikn Nuggit TikTok animated series followers format episode length". Started October 2020; over 300 shorts; 8 to 10 million followers across platforms and about a billion views; each short around 15 to 20 seconds; now being developed as a longer series with Frederator (Animation Magazine, Playback, from June 2023). The search found nothing on a jingle; the description of the comedy style is my own knowledge.
findings.how_for_us: Our 28 seconds is at the long end for a sketch. Keep the pilot as written but also cut a 20-second version for testing (shots 4 and 5 as one beat, shot 2 at three seconds) and compare completion. In every film each friend's trait is shown by an action, without words, inside the first three seconds: Timo's whole-arm point, Luna's hand on something too big, too tasty or too furry. The cat is the third character with one trait: never impressed, except once.
findings.risk: The cute food-animal tone skews to early teens; ours has to stay 18 to 30 (streetwear, adult bodies, football). A shorter cut may lose shot 5, the moment Timo starts to enjoy it, which is the warm beat the client asked for.

findings.what: Openly AI accounts that last say so themselves, in the handle, bio or caption, with humour and without apology, and then get on with the character.
findings.evidence: Search: "Granny Spills AI influencer how made catchphrase disclosure". Granny Spills (Blur Studios, two creators in their twenties in New York): 400,000 TikTok and 1 million Instagram followers in her first weeks (Bloomberg, 23 October 2025); catchphrase "Flowers die, honey. My Chanel bags are forever" with nearly a million likes; a caption reading "Yes I am AI". @ai.cinema021 had "ai" in its handle. Search "brand AI-generated ad backlash 2026": Almond Breeze (Marketing Brew, 28 January 2026) said "AI slop" comments were answered by other viewers because the ad made fun of itself. Search "Gen Z attitude AI-generated content 2026": IAB 2026 found clear disclosure is the third-highest driver of attention to AI ads, after high-quality visuals and being funny.
findings.how_for_us: Account line: "Two best friends. Football trips abroad. Animated with AI, written and directed by people." The platform AI label on every post, as the bible already demands. One pinned comment under the pilot in a human voice: "Yes, it's AI animation. The jokes, the designs and the song are ours. Big Yellow is real to us." No AI talk inside the film.
findings.risk: Too much AI talk makes AI the subject: one line, then back to the friends. "Made by people" is only safe where it is true (writing, design, voices, music); overclaiming is worse than silence.

findings.what: What separates an "AI series" from "AI slop" for platforms and press: a person writes, performs and directs, the world stays consistent, and every episode is different. The reference is Neural Viz: one filmmaker writes the scripts, storyboards the shots and performs every character himself through performance-capture tools.
findings.evidence: Search: "Neural Viz AI series Monoverse creator". WIRED profile, October 2025, "The Future of AI Isn't Just Slop": Josh Wallace Kerrigan, Runway Act-One and Act-Two, several spin-off shows in one universe, hundreds of thousands of views per video on YouTube and millions on TikTok and Instagram; no 2026 update found. Search: "YouTube Shorts AI slop channels removed 2026": by late January 2026, 16 of the 100 most-subscribed slop channels had been deleted or emptied (about 4.7 billion views and 35 million subscribers; Kapwing, Tubefilter 29 January 2026); the policy on inauthentic, mass-produced content judges whole channels. Hiebing research, June 2026: Gen Z trusts brands that show their work.
findings.how_for_us: Leave human fingerprints where viewers can find them: credits in the post text ("Written by ..., music by ..."); real voice performances for Timo and Luna if at all possible (Luna laughing in the middle of words is what synthetic voices do worst); and one making-of post in the second week showing the character sheets, Big Yellow's reference sheet and the theme being built in layers. Change the place and the big object in every film so the channel never looks like a template.
findings.risk: A making-of that shows prompts and tool logos invites the argument instead of ending it. A channel of near-identical films (same seven beats, same street) could be read as mass-produced; variety of object and location is the protection. I could not verify how the series' voices are actually produced.

findings.what: The labelling rules per platform as of autumn 2026.
findings.evidence: Searches: "TikTok AI-generated content label rules 2026", "tubefilter TikTok AI transparency tools July 2026", "Instagram AI info label 2026", "YouTube altered or synthetic content disclosure animation", "EU AI Act Article 50 August 2026". TikTok: realistic AI content must be labelled; over 3 billion videos labelled by July 2026 (1.3 billion in March); invisible watermarks; since November 2025 a "Manage Topics" slider lets users see less AI content; Tubefilter, 14 July 2026, cites a 2025 study in which labels did not significantly change engagement. Instagram: from 31 August 2026 an "AI-generated profile" label; accounts featuring AI-generated people without it stop being recommended to non-followers, labelled accounts are not penalised, creators who merely use AI tools are exempt (TechRepublic, Khaleej Times). YouTube: since May 2026 it detects and labels undisclosed AI itself; photoreal content gets an overlay on Shorts, stylised or animated content usually only a note in the expanded description (sources differ). EU AI Act Article 50 duties for those who publish AI content apply from 2 August 2026 and were not delayed (Jones Walker, Cloud Security Alliance).
findings.how_for_us: Switch the AI label on at upload on all three platforms for the pilot and for every cut-down. Before the Instagram account opens, decide with the client whether to add the profile-level label: our leads are toy figures, not fake people, so it is probably not required, but adding it removes any risk of being throttled. The stylised toy look sits on the safe side of every rule because it never pretends to be real footage.
findings.risk: These rules change month to month and my sources are trade press, not the platforms' own help pages: check each help centre in the week of posting. The TikTok slider means some viewers will see less labelled AI content; that is the price of not being taken down. This is not legal advice.

findings.what: The audience climate around AI video in late 2026: feeds are saturated, young viewers are wary, children's cartoons are the most polluted category, and the best-liked comment under an AI post is often the call-out.
findings.evidence: Search: "Kapwing TikTok AI slop report": June 2026, 294 of the first 500 videos shown to a fresh TikTok account (59%) were AI slop, against about 21% on YouTube Shorts; in the Kids category 57.4%; under #cartoonkids 97 of 100. The BBC's Joe Tidy, quoted in that report: likes on AI-backlash comments often exceed those on the post. Search: "Gen Z attitude AI-generated content brands survey 2026": Attest, February 2026, 1,000 US Gen Z adults: 41% actively dislike AI content, 72% negative or cautious; IAB 2026: 45% of Gen Z and millennials feel positive about AI ads while 82% of ad executives believe they do; Rival Technologies, August 2026 (press release): nearly three in four Gen Z say they have punished a brand over AI. Search: "brand AI-generated animated ad backlash 2026": McDonald's Netherlands pulled its AI Christmas ad (December 2025); Coca-Cola's 2025 AI holiday ad was called soulless; Svedka's Super Bowl 2026 AI robots fell flat; Quip's ad made without AI (April 2026) was still accused of being AI. Several surveys are vendor-sponsored: treat as direction, not precision.
findings.how_for_us: Three consequences. (1) Frame one must look art-directed, not generated: limited palette, adult bodies, streetwear, real sunlight, nothing that resembles the kids' cartoon slop filling the feed. (2) Zero visible faults: the bible's fault gate is the most important of the three, because one melting hand becomes the top comment. (3) Give the comments something better than AI to talk about: a side to pick (Plan or No Plan), an open question (what is in Big Yellow?) and a naming job (the cat has no name on screen, so ask viewers to name it).
findings.risk: Some "AI slop" comments are certain; deleting them or arguing makes it worse. Keeping the brand to the last two seconds is right: every burned case above was an advert.

findings.what: Football feeds in 2026: the World Cup summer was flooded with AI anime of real stars, and the one toy-style football film everybody liked was LEGO's.
findings.evidence: Search: "Complex World Cup 2026 AI anime videos Mbappe Haaland Messi": AI anime videos of Messi, Mbappe and Haaland were among the biggest viral trends of the tournament (Complex; El Comercio), including a full mini-series by @DiabloNemesis; Euronews, 8 July 2026: "AI's biggest World Cup star is a fake Erling Haaland", with dozens of accounts profiting. No reliable view counts found. Search: "LEGO World Cup 2026 ad fans react AI": the Wieden+Kennedy film ("Everyone Wants a Piece", early April 2026) passed 75 million views in days, was praised for comedy and music, and carried a small "Animation used" line; when a behind-the-scenes clip showed stand-ins, fans wrote "I knew it was AI".
findings.how_for_us: Take the lane nobody is in: fans, not players. No star lookalikes, no kits, no badges (already in the bible). Each film should hit one fan truth hard enough to be sent to a friend with "this is you": the friend who packs for a month is the right pilot. Football fans call out AI quickly, so be labelled first and funny first.
findings.risk: Anything resembling a real player, kit or stadium invites a takedown or a legal letter. The World Cup wave is over; any nod to it would look late.

findings.what: The handmade look as the answer to glossy AI video: clay, felt, vinyl-toy and miniature-set styles are used to signal "someone made this", and collectible art toys are now mainstream for adults.
findings.evidence: Search: "claymation OR stop motion OR felt AI video trend TikTok 2026": tool sellers (Opus, Lovart, 2026) describe claymation AI as a "cozy counter-trend" to slop fatigue, with cues such as thumbprint texture, slight imperfections, miniature sets and about 12 frames a second; this is vendor material, not independent data. Searches: "Labubu Pop Mart art toy animation series" and "vinyl toy / art toy style AI characters video trend 2026": Pop Mart and Sony announced a Labubu feature film on 19 March 2026; the AI "toy figure" picture style was among the most shared of 2025 and 2026 (vendor guides). I found no named breakout account using an art-toy video style: the lane looks open, which also means unproven.
findings.how_for_us: Push material truth so the film reads as made, not rendered: visible coarse weave on Luna's shirt, matte vinyl skin, scuffs on her trainers, a moulding seam and small scratches on Big Yellow, hard real-sun shadows on the cobbles, dust from the wheels in shot 7. Movement slightly snappy, never floaty.
findings.risk: The "action figure in a box" meme was spring 2025: no packaging, no blister-pack jokes. Too much toy stiffness kills the warmth of the faces, which the client needs most. The Labubu craze is cooling, so do not lean on blind-box culture.

top3: Open on voice and sound inside the first second and a half. In shot 1, start Timo's "Luna. It's one night!" over the bump of the suitcase and let his eyes travel and his arm sink after the line, not before it. Every character format that grew (vlog characters, chant characters, numbered micro-episodes) has voice or music on the first frame.

Fix one sound-and-cut signature and never vary it: "No. No, no, no." in the same four-beat rhythm, music down to the tick-tock, hard cut on the downbeat with the five claps, the friends' movements landing on the beat. Publish it as a named original sound. This is the series' catchphrase, its recognisable audio and the part viewers can reuse.

Be openly AI and visibly human from the first post: platform AI label on TikTok, Reels and Shorts, one line in the bio, one pinned comment, human credits in the post text, and a comment section seeded with character questions (Plan or No Plan? Name the cat. What is in Big Yellow?). The year's biggest AI series was reported off TikTok in 15 days, partly for unlabelled AI.
avoid: Posting without the AI label, or answering 'is this AI?' evasively. Fruit Love Island lost about 12 of 22 episodes to mass reports citing unlabelled AI and fake engagement.
The brainrot, talking-fruit, pet-drama or cheating-plot look and tone. It is tagged as slop, it skews to children, and absurd plots are what the client could not follow last time.
Anything that looks like a kids' cartoon (nursery colours, baby proportions, squeaky voices). Kapwing found 57% of TikTok's Kids category and 97 of 100 #cartoonkids videos were AI slop.
Real players, lookalikes, kits, badges or anime versions of stars. The World Cup AI wave was full of them and it is both late and legally unsafe.
Chart or trending commercial sounds on the brand account, and making Timo and Luna dance to trends. A business account is limited to cleared music, and dance trends date in weeks.
Numbers, 'Part 2', 'previously' or cliffhangers inside the film, and micro-drama lengths of two to four minutes.
A selfie 'hey guys' vlog. The AI vlog format peaked in summer 2025.
Reused clips, the same street every time, or reposted loops. YouTube's policy on mass-produced content judges the whole channel.
Bought or fake engagement, comment-bait strings and 'tag your friend'.
Deleting or arguing with 'AI slop' comments, and claiming more human work than is true.
Any visible generation fault. Viewers screenshot mismatched limbs and melted hands, and that becomes the top comment.
Toy-in-a-box packaging jokes (the spring 2025 action-figure meme) and leaning on the Labubu craze.
Launching on TikTok alone. Post to Reels and Shorts the same day so one takedown or throttle cannot end the series.
