findings.what: Planner friend versus go-with-the-flow friend skits ("Type A / Type B friend"). A long-running TikTok and Reels format in which a friendship group, usually filmed on holiday, plays up the friction between the friend who books and schedules everything (Type A) and the easygoing one who just turns up (Type B). The typical scene: the relaxed friend asks "can we just go with the flow?" and the planner's face does the rest. In 2026 the same split came back as the "round or square" test (rounds are chaotic, squares are orderly). This is the Timo and Luna premise.
findings.evidence: Searches: "type A type B friend travel TikTok trend planner friend chaos friend" and "Dazed Are you a Type A or Type B friend". Dazed article dated 19 June 2025. The Independent describes satirical friend-group videos "usually filmed on holiday" and one holiday video with more than 2 million views. A Yahoo piece cites a Dionna May skit with over 6 million viewers. Paris Select Book (2026, single source) reports a "round or square" video about a laid-back friend and a perfectionist friend at 5.3 million views. Bustle names "planner friends" versus "Venmo friends". YourTango ran "not a Type B friend, just a bad friend", which shows the backlash.
findings.how_for_us: Never say the labels on screen. Put them in the post text, where the bible already puts context: "Type A friend. Type B friend. One suitcase. Which one are you?" The four-second beat that carries it without words is already the pilot's first frame: Timo's whole arm pointing up the hill, Luna's flat hand proudly on the giant suitcase. For later films: Timo points straight ahead with his whole arm, Luna is already drifting sideways towards food; he looks at his arm, then at her, and lowers it.
findings.risk: The Type A/B wording peaked in 2025 and "round or square" may be gone in weeks, so the labels belong only in post text, which can change per post. The backlash ("Type B is just a bad friend") means Luna must be right in her turn and never a flake who costs Timo something. The bible already demands this; the scripts must keep it.

findings.what: The "Go go go" trend. A current TikTok format: an audio of someone repeating "go, go, go, go" with rising impatience, laid as a voiceover over footage of a person taking their time. It plays the inner monologue of someone staying polite while a slow person tests them. Example captions in the roundups include the friend who says they will be "right back".
findings.evidence: Searches: "Ramdam TikTok trends November 2026 Go go go voiceover" and a follow-up on how creators use it. Ramdam's trend post dated 10 November 2026 (a marketing blog) describes the inner-monologue use. New Engen's November 2026 page and a Substack trend report ("Get Out of This Neighbourhood, Go Go Go & My Best") describe a lip-sync version of the same audio. No view counts were found.
findings.how_for_us: The pilot's shot 2 is this trend already: the suitcase barely moves and a cat overtakes them while only Timo's eyes follow it. Sharpen it in sound, not picture: let Timo's tick-tock layer double its speed for those four seconds against the slow grind of the wheels, then snap back when the cat looks round. A four-second beat for a later film: Luna crouches to greet the cat; Timo stands behind her with a fixed polite smile and only his yellow-watch hand tapping on the beat. Post text for that film: "Me, staying very calm, while she says hello to every cat."
findings.risk: Do not use the audio itself. It is a third-party sound, the bible bans voiceover, and a sound trend like this lasts two or three weeks, which is less than the time needed to generate a film. Only the situation is safe to borrow.

findings.what: Short synced two-person dances, the biggest duo format this week. "Ba Ba Ba Dance": two friends, four parts (side by side, one solo, the other solo, synced finish). "Shoulder Carry": one sits on the other's shoulders, then they swap on the lyric "cause I'm the one". "Dame Hombro": fast shoulder pops with knee bends. There is also a three-person routine to a sped-up, chipmunk-voice "You Spin Me Round".
findings.evidence: Searches: "viralremix TikTok trends November 13 2026 chart", "Ba Ba Ba Dance duo trend routine explained", "Dame Hombro TikTok dance trend". The viralremix.org daily chart for 13 November 2026 (an AI video tool's chart) lists Ba Ba Ba Dance at about 42,300 new videos a day, down 6 percent and marked "peak", and Shoulder Carry at 14,800 a day, down 20 percent, also "peak". The Ba Ba Ba origin (posted 2 October 2026; the sound is a fan mashup of Tori Kelly's "Don't You Worry 'Bout a Thing" from the film Sing with a Ca$h Out track) comes only from AI-video vendor blogs, so it is unverified. Tokchart: "Dame Hombro" released 7 October 2026, about 193,300 videos. The chipmunk dance is from New Engen's November 2026 page.
findings.how_for_us: Do not copy a named routine. Borrow the structure, which is the bible's own music logic: side by side, her move (a little late), his move (on the beat), then locked together. Build one "Plan, No Plan" move on the theme's five-clap: two shoulder pops (Timo on the beat, Luna a touch late), then three claps together. Three seconds, upper body only. The Shoulder Carry swap is a ready picture laugh for a later film about seeing over a crowd: Timo offers his shoulders, Luna says "No", hard cut, tall Timo is sitting on short Luna's shoulders and she is perfectly fine.
findings.risk: Both chart leaders are already falling and will be over before a generated film is finished. Copying them with their sounds is a rights problem (the Ba Ba Ba sound is an uncleared mashup). Long choreography is on the production "risky" list: anything over three seconds or with footwork will break, or look like a brand trying to dance. A lift must be a cut, never shown.

findings.what: The rule that decides what "trendy music" can mean: a brand account cannot use chart songs or most trending sounds. TikTok's and Instagram's music licences cover personal posts, not brand content. Brands are limited to the Commercial Music Library (over 500,000 cleared tracks, without the big hits) or to music they own.
findings.evidence: Search: "brands sued using trending songs TikTok Instagram posts lawsuit 2026 commercial music library". UMG and Concord sued the fashion brand Quince in April 2026 over 138 works, up to 20.7 million dollars (Music Business Worldwide, The Fashion Law). Warner sued Crumbl over 159 songs (reported settled in 2026), DSW in May 2025 over more than 200 tracks, PacSun in December 2025 and the owner of Ray-Ban and Oakley; Sony also sued DSW. For reference, what is charting now: New Engen's US chart for 30 October to 5 November 2026 lists Harry Styles "Coming Up Roses", Tate McRae "Housewife" and Steve Lacy "The Feeling"; Tokchart's worldwide chart of 7 November 2026 lists "Paper Moon Static" and "Montagem da Chupeta".
findings.how_for_us: Keep the series theme "Tick Tock Clap" and make it behave like a trending sound: the tick-tock recognisable within the first second, the full groove landing exactly on the "No" cut as the drop, and the five-clap (clap, clap, clap-clap-clap) as the part people can copy. Publish the 15-second hook as a named original sound on the account so other people can put it under their own trip videos. Tell the client in one line: "trendy" means our own track built like a trend, because a chart song on a brand account is a lawsuit.
findings.risk: The client may expect a song he recognises. If anyone "just adds" a trending sound in the app at upload, the whole account is exposed. A made-to-order afro-house track can sound like stock music; it needs one rough, human hook (the three-note "oh-oh-oh" from young voices) to be something people want to reuse.

findings.what: Fan rituals, not match action, are the football-trip content that travelled furthest in 2026: travelling fans doing one simple thing together in a foreign town. The clearest case is Norway's "Viking Row": fans sit close together in a line and pull their arms back and forth to a drum beat, as if rowing a longship. It was done on escalators, in streets and in stands. The other was Scotland's fans taking over Boston with songs and bagpipes.
findings.evidence: Searches: "World Cup 2026 TikTok fan trends viral fan travel content", "TikTok newsroom FIFA World Cup 2026 1 trillion views" and "Viking Row World Cup 2026 Norway fans". TikTok's newsroom reports 1.2 trillion views of tournament content and names Scotland's Boston takeover and Norway's Viking Row as the fan-driven moments. One search summary credits Viking Row with over 172 million TikTok views. Explained by NPR (25 June 2026), The National (28 June 2026), STV and Good Morning America; the players joined in after a win over Senegal. TikTok also reports that 72 percent of its users enjoy fan-made videos (a company figure).
findings.how_for_us: The pilot already seats the friends one behind the other on Big Yellow. In shot 5, the turn, let the joy be a shared move and not only a raised fist: Timo, now loving it, pulls both arms back twice in time with the claps and Luna does the same in front of him, a two-stroke "row" on a suitcase. A football fan recognises it at once; anyone else sees two friends rowing a suitcase downhill. If the sync does not generate cleanly, the safe version is Timo throwing his arms up in the same V as Luna on the first clap: he has joined her way, in one picture.
findings.risk: Viking Row belongs to one national team. Anything beyond a two-stroke nod (a drum, a chant, helmets, that team's colours) breaks the "no real club or nation" rule and invites "you took our thing" comments. By mid-2027 it may feel as dated as the 2016 thunderclap. Two figures moving in sync at speed is a moderate generation risk, so it needs a fallback ready.

findings.what: The half-and-half scarf problem. In football culture the "half-and-half scarf" (one half one team, the other half the opponent) is the most mocked matchday item: regular fans treat it as the mark of a tourist. The series' trip scarf is half teal and half coral, so football viewers will read it as a half-and-half.
findings.evidence: Search: "half-and-half scarf football fans mock tourists backlash 2026". A Change.org petition created 19 January 2026 asks for them to be banned in the home sections at Old Trafford. West Ham banned them for a derby against Tottenham (beIN Sports, 11 September 2025). FourFourTwo calls it "the unacceptable yet unavoidable football match day accessory". The Anfield Wrap ties it to the "football tourist" argument.
findings.how_for_us: Own it before the comments do. In the post text or the first pinned comment: "Yes, it is a half-and-half scarf. Half him, half her." It is a free conversation starter with exactly the audience we want, and it explains the scarf as friendship, not two clubs. In a later film the local scarf seller can look at their scarf, look at them and laugh kindly (the local is the generous one). The pilot picture needs no change.
findings.risk: Left unaddressed, the top comment from real match-goers will be "tourists", which undercuts the brief's "football-trip true". Over-explained, it becomes an in-joke that second-language viewers outside Britain do not get. One line is enough.

findings.what: Comment prompts that work in the friend niche: a two-way identity question tied to one specific habit, not a request to tag. The working shapes are "which one are you?" between two named types, "always that ONE friend", and "who planned the trip?", where a group shows who did the work and who only paid. Asking people to "tag a friend" is treated as engagement bait.
findings.evidence: Searches: "who planned the trip TikTok trend friends vacation", "tag a friend engagement bait TikTok Instagram algorithm 2026" and "TikTok trend friends trip 2026 the friend who skit". USA Today (syndicated on AOL) on "Who planned the trip?" videos about who does and does not plan. Bustle on "planner friends" versus "Venmo friends". A TikTok discover page of "always that ONE friend" trip-planning skits tagged #comedyskit #friends #girlstrip. Marketing glossaries list "tag a friend" as bait and claim reach cuts of 50 to 90 percent; no platform source confirms that figure.
findings.how_for_us: Keep the bible's "Plan or No Plan: which one are you?" but tie it to the habit in the picture: "One night. One suitcase this big. Plan or No Plan: which one are you?" Pin one in-character comment from the account: "Timo here. It was ONE night." Add the series' standing question as a second comment: "What is in Big Yellow?" When the habit is that specific, people name their own friend without being asked.
findings.risk: Every brand uses "which one are you?", so it only works attached to a concrete picture. A pinned in-character comment reads as trying too hard if it is longer than one line. Never write "tag", "share" or "comment below".

findings.what: Five two-friend interactions of three to five seconds each, readable with the sound off, taken from formats in circulation: sharing or swapping food, arms too full to help ("Sorry I can't, my hands are full"), rock-paper-scissors to settle who does the unpleasant job, the slow friend and the waiting friend, and the tall-short contrast.
findings.evidence: Searches: "SocialBee TikTok trends you can't miss November 2026", "rock paper scissors food challenge TikTok trend friends October 2026" and "TikTok trend friends trip 2026 the friend who". SocialBee's page dated 5 November 2026 lists "Sorry I can't, my hands are full" (stack things in your arms until you can hold no more) and an August "Turn me around" shared-meal swap. The Virlo tracker of 29 October 2026 showed the rock-paper-scissors food challenge at 54 creators that week, up from 2, and predicted it would be over by 1 November. The beats themselves are my own construction from these formats, not found videos.
findings.how_for_us: (1) Food: Luna holds a snack on a stick under Timo's nose, he shakes his head "No", hard cut, his cheeks are full and he is holding two. (2) Hands full: Timo holds out Big Yellow's handle; Luna's arms are stacked to her chin with food and scarves, she shrugs; he turns his eyes to the camera. (3) Rock-paper-scissors: three fist beats on the tick-tock, Luna wins, hard cut, Timo pushes the suitcase with Luna sitting on it, eating. (4) Walking: Timo strides out of frame in a straight line while Luna drifts to the cat; two seconds later Timo walks back into frame backwards. (5) The lean: after the laugh Luna drops her head against Timo's arm (she reaches his shoulder) and he pats her head twice on the beat.
findings.risk: The food challenge itself is already over and involved people being sick; borrow only the game. Rock-paper-scissors needs readable hands, a known weak point of generated video, so frame it large and show one throw only. Beat 5 must stay brother-and-sister: a pat, never a held look. A food hand-over is always a cut.

findings.what: Travel formats measured as working this month are built on withholding and on the unfamous place: "dismiss the famous pick, push the lesser-known one", and "hold back the place name until the final seconds". A related joke format, "We can't all be in...", celebrates ordinary places over postcard ones.
findings.evidence: Search: "tryvolume travel TikTok trends this week November 2026 viral formats hooks". Volume's travel page, measured 8 November 2026 on 711 posts: the "lesser-known pick" format was used by 15 accounts at a median of 9 times their usual reach; "place name held to the end" by 15 accounts at a median of 7 times; a Google Earth zoom-in by 9 accounts. "We can't all be in..." is from SocialBee's trend page, where it sits under an August 2026 heading. Small sample, one vendor.
findings.how_for_us: The series has an invented town with no name, which fits "withhold the place": never name it, and once, in a post text, ask "Which town does this look like to you?" The pilot already holds the destination back until shot 3, when the stadium appears in the gap between the two friends. Protect that reveal: in shot 1 show only the four floodlight masts over the hill, never the bowl. A post line for a later film: "Not the famous stadium. The one up the hill."
findings.risk: Travel viewers reward real places and real street food. A model town cannot compete as travel advice, so a film must never be framed as a tip or a guide. A guessing prompt irritates if people feel there is no answer; use it once, not on every post.

findings.what: "How Different Our Lives Are". A two-person format from late summer: short clips through one day, cut back and forth, showing how differently two friends or siblings live the same day. Many creators now play both roles alone.
findings.evidence: Search: "How Different Our Lives Are TikTok trend two friends explained sound". Ramdam's trend guide lists it under 3 August 2026 with the sound credited as "original sound - Daryl Hall & John Oates". A TikTok discover page was last updated 7 September 2026. NapoleonCat and Anijam still carry it on their "current trends" pages. The peak was August to September, so it is late.
findings.how_for_us: Not for the pilot. As a 12 to 15 second second film for the account: the same trip morning in alternating two-second shots. Timo: scarf knotted, watch checked, first at the empty station. Luna: asleep, then toast in her mouth, then running. Last shot: both reach Big Yellow at the same moment and do the five-clap. Full-frame cuts, no split screen, our own theme: his tick-tock under his shots, her log drum under hers, both together on the last shot.
findings.risk: The trend is two to three months old and its sound is a commercial recording we cannot use; sold as "the trend" it will look late. As plain parallel editing it is timeless. It needs about six new start pictures, so it costs nearly as much as an episode.

findings.what: How football-trip posts are labelled. The niche words are "away days" (British for travelling to watch your team), "groundhopping" (collecting stadiums) and "matchday". Travel companies moved into this space in 2026, so the niche is filling with adverts that look like adverts.
findings.evidence: Searches: "away day football trip TikTok trend 2026 fans travel abroad", "football away day vlog TikTok format 2026" and "football TikTok hashtags 2026 #awaydays #groundhopping". TikTok has an "Away Days Football" discover page. G Adventures launched "Away Games" football trips with first departures in October 2026, and Outlook Traveller calls sport-led "fan voyage" travel the biggest travel trend of 2026. A hashtag tool shows #groundhopping at about 454,000 posts, but that is Instagram data. I found no reliable TikTok view counts for these tags, and the tag choice below is my own knowledge, not a search result.
findings.how_for_us: Post text is one plain sentence about the situation, then three or four tags, never a wall: "When your friend packs for one night. #awaydays #footballtrip #matchday #travelwithfriends". The account line stays "Two best friends. Football trips abroad." Keep the same tags in the same order on every post so the series can be found as a set.
findings.risk: "Away days" is British club slang and its regulars are protective; a toy-town brand series under that tag will draw a few "tourist" comments, so always pair it with a neutral tag. Do not use any tournament, league or club tag: it is stale since July and a trademark risk. Never "soccer".

findings.what: Check on the pilot's own premise: the friend who overpacks, and riding a suitcase. Neither is a named current trend. Packing content on TikTok is mostly hacks for avoiding bag fees (fishing vests, pillowcases, duty-free bags); the overpacker appears as a recognisable type, not a format. Riding a suitcase is known from motorised ride-on cases that celebrities posted and that some places restrict.
findings.evidence: Searches: "overpacker friend vs carry-on friend TikTok trend suitcase for one night viral 2026" and "riding suitcase downhill TikTok viral friends ride-on suitcase trend airport ban". Results were packing hacks from 2023 to 2025 (one fishing-vest video at 1.8 million views, one pillowcase video at 24.9 million) and one self-described overpacker, @marypoppinspacked, at over 655,000 views. No downhill suitcase-ride trend was found. Japan fined a rider of a motorised suitcase in Osaka in 2024 and Singapore's Changi Airport bans riding them.
findings.how_for_us: Treat the pilot as evergreen, not as a trend ride, and say so to the client: its trend value comes from the music hook, the synced move and the post text, not from the story. The line people will quote is the last one, "Timo. This is the small one", so it must be clean, alone on screen and followed by a full second of Luna's laugh before the card. The bible's post line "When your friend packs for one night." is the right one.
findings.risk: A downhill ride on a suitcase could be copied by a child. The art-toy world keeps it clearly a cartoon; never add a prompt such as "try it" and never show a fall. Claiming the pilot "uses a trend" when it does not would repeat the trust problem with this client.

top3: No chart song. Make the series theme do the job of a trending sound: tick-tock recognisable in the first second, the full groove landing as the drop exactly on the "No" cut, the five-clap (clap, clap, clap-clap-clap) as the part people can copy, and the 15-second hook published as a named original sound on the account. Tell the client in one line why: brand accounts are being sued for using trending songs (Quince, April 2026, up to 20.7 million dollars).

One synced two-friend move inside the story, under three seconds, with no words. In shot 5 (the turn) Timo joins Luna's move on the claps: two rowing pulls on the suitcase, a nod to the 2026 "Viking Row" fan ritual, or at minimum the same arms-up V as hers. This answers "interactions between the characters" and "trends of right now" in one picture that reads with the sound off, and it replaces copying a dance that will be dead before the film is generated.

The post package, because that is where the trend words can live without breaking the film: "One night. One suitcase this big. Plan or No Plan: which one are you?", a pinned "What is in Big Yellow?", one line owning the scarf ("Yes, it is a half-and-half. Half him, half her."), three or four tags (#awaydays #footballtrip #matchday #travelwithfriends), the AI label, and never "tag a friend".
avoid: Any licensed or trending commercial audio on the brand account, including adding a trending sound in the app at upload. Platform music licences do not cover brands; Quince, Crumbl, DSW, PacSun and the Ray-Ban owner were all sued in 2025 and 2026.

Copying this week's named trends literally: the Ba Ba Ba dance, Dame Hombro, the Tate McRae "Housewife" dance, the "Go go go" audio. Both duo-dance chart leaders were already falling on 13 November 2026 and will be over before a generated film is finished.

Dated travel memes: the "Nothing beats a Jet2 holiday" sound and "airport theory" are 2025 trends; the rock-paper-scissors food challenge was predicted dead by 1 November 2026 and is remembered for people being sick.
"Tag a friend who...", "share this", "comment below". It is widely classed as engagement bait and the bible already forbids it. Ask a concrete either-or question instead.

Saying "Type A", "Type B", "round" or "square" in dialogue or captions inside the film. They are label trends with a short life and a backlash ("Type B is just a bad friend"). Luna must never be the flake who costs Timo something.

Copying a real fan ritual in full (the Viking Row with its drum and chant, the thunderclap) or using tournament, league or club hashtags. It breaks the "no real club or nation" rule, risks trademark trouble and invites "you took our thing" comments.
Leaving the half-teal, half-coral scarf unexplained. To match-going fans a half-and-half scarf means "tourist"; one line of post text turns it into the series' joke.

Characters performing for a phone or a camera at the ground. Football writers and fans mock the "Concourse Army" who film themselves instead of watching the match; the friends must be seen to care about the game (its light and roar on their faces).
Alcohol as the fun of the trip. The Scotland fans "drinking Boston dry" was a real viral story, but the bible forbids it and it narrows where the films can be promoted.
Framing any film as a travel tip or guide. The travel formats that win are real places and real street food; a model town cannot compete there and will read as an advert.

Telling the client the pilot "rides a trend". The overpacker and the suitcase ride are evergreen situations, not current trends. Say plainly that the trend value sits in the music hook, the synced move and the post text.

Template sameness and a missing AI label. Platforms are acting against templated AI video (YouTube removed 16 channels in January 2026 under its inauthentic-content rule; TikTok's rule centres on disclosure), so every film keeps the label and must look designed, with real interaction: eye contact, touch, overlapping laughter.

changes: MUSIC, the client's first request ('trendy, fun music'). The theme 'Tick Tock Clap' stays at 120 beats a minute, because the sound research puts afro house with a log-drum bounce inside what this year's feed sounds like. It is hardened so that it sounds like autumn 2026 and not like stock music: the groove starts in the first half second, the log drum gets a mid-range knock that survives a phone speaker, a pitched one-syllable vocal chop answers the claps, an organ stab pumps with the kick, the claps are real hands in a dry room, and the drop is set up by a dead stop, not a riser. No chart song in any form: two researchers found that labels are suing brands for exactly that, and only a sound we own can become our trend.

THE DROP NOW SITS EXACTLY ON THE 'NO' CUT (asked for by the sound, formats and series research). The sound researcher's arithmetic showed that in version 2 the drop fell on the wrong beat. The shots are re-cut to 5 / 3.5 / 4 / 2 / 3 / 3 / 6 seconds: six bars of build end at 12.0, the music stops dead for one beat, the full groove and Timo's scream land on the cut at 12.5, the 'oh-oh-oh' enters on a downbeat at 14.5 and the hug starts on a downbeat at 20.5. Plain hard cut, no speed ramp, no effect.

LUNA ANSWERS BACK FROM SECOND 3.5 (client: 'interactions between the characters'). In version 2 she had one line, at second 24, with her mouth hidden. Now she answers his first line with 'Yes! One night!' and pats her suitcase twice. Her word is 'Yes', his word is 'No', and on the ride he shouts her word, so the film reads Yes, No, Yes (formats research: the 'No' that turns into a 'Yes').

'TRUST ME.' IS ADDED BEFORE THE 'NO' (client: interactions; series and sound research: one fixed sound bite, identical in every film, that viewers can reuse). The offer is two words and the answer is four: 'Trust me.' / 'No. No, no, no.' Then a beat of nothing, then the drop and the scream that turns into a laugh. The same seven seconds return in every film, whichever friend says which half, and are published as a named original sound.

THE 'NO' IS NOW PLAYED BETWEEN THE TWO, AS A RHYTHM (series research: movements land on the beat; formats research: solo, solo, together). He says 'No.', she answers with two pats on the empty seat, he says 'no, no, no'. Her two pats and his three quick no's are already the five-clap of the theme (clap, clap, clap-clap-clap), which then returns as real claps after the cut and on the card.

ONE GESTURE TRAVELS THROUGH THE FILM AND ENDS AS A TOUCH (client: interactions; niche research: eye contact, touch and overlapping laughter are what make a film look made and not templated). Luna's pat-pat appears three times: on her suitcase (proud), on the empty seat (the offer) and at the end on Timo's flat-top, which she can reach only because he is on his knees. Version 2 had no touch between them at all.

SHOT 2, FOUR EYES (formats research: the reaction close-up; niche research: the slow friend and the waiting friend, the situation under the current 'Go go go' trend). Both pairs of eyes now follow the cat together with the heads still, then find each other. In the sound, Timo's tick-tock runs at double speed against the slow wheels. Only the situation is borrowed; the trend audio is not used.

SHOT 5, THE DOUBLE V (niche research: one synced two-friend move under three seconds with no words; formats research: a pair of animated characters spreads when it owns one move). Timo's single fist becomes both arms up in the same V as Luna's, his V above hers, and she twists round to laugh up at him. I did not take the two-stroke rowing move that the niche researcher offered: it belongs to one national team's fans and the bible rules that out. Plan B is the tested version 2 picture (one fist up, one hand on her shoulder).
SHOT 6: both shout 'Byeee!' together as they pass the cat (client: interactions). It is sound only, so it adds no picture risk, and it answers the cat's 'mrrp' from the uphill.

SHOT 7 ENDS ON THE REVEAL AND ON A REACTION (formats research: end on the reveal and loop tight; niche research: the last line clean and alone, then a full second of laugh; series research: the third friend behind the camera should be felt once per film). The hug is now two clips of one idea: the tested wide picture for 'I love this suitcase.', then a closer one in which Luna pats his head, says 'Timo. This is the small one.' and his eyes snap open straight into the camera. Her laugh runs on under the card. The card keeps its two seconds.

THE HOOK LINE: YES, ONE LINE (formats research, first recommendation; client: 'what works on TikTok'). 'When your friend packs for one night' at the top of the frame for the first 1.8 seconds only. The brief allows one line; bible rule 9 ('no header') has to be changed to allow it, and the earlier team rejected it for reading load. So it has conditions: it is gone before the first caption, there are never two texts at once, the silent gate is run with it covered, and if a test viewer says it looks like an advert or a meme page it comes off and nothing else in the film changes.

FIRST VOICE AT 2.0 SECONDS, not at about 3 (series research: voice or music on the first frame). The groove and the bump of the suitcase start on frame one, Timo speaks on the bar line as the hook leaves, and his arm sinks while he speaks, not before.

NOT TAKEN, AND WHY. The 0.8-second flash-forward opening (formats research, offered as a test only): it shows the ride twice and breaks the order of cause and effect, which is what the client could not follow last time. The 20-second cut (series research): a test version only, because it loses the moment Timo starts to enjoy it. Any trending song, the 'Go go go' audio, the named dances, split screens, speed ramps, 'POV', slang and 'tag a friend': the research itself rules each of them out as late, unlicensed, heavy to read or a fault risk.

WHAT MUST CHANGE IN THE BIBLE FOR THIS VERSION: rule 9 (one hook line allowed in the first two seconds; six short captions instead of four, still one text at a time and at most two per shot); the shot 7 note 'nobody touches the other' (one head pat); and Luna now has two lines with visible lips (shots 1 and 3), where version 2 had none. Each of these has a plan B written into its shot. The ride clips are still made first as the go or no-go.

HONEST LIMITS. Version 2 is the cut that 9 of 10 cold viewers understood; version 3 has not been tested. The story, its order, the seven shots and the silent retell sentence are unchanged, but the strip gate and the silent gate must be run again before the clips are paid for. The story itself is not a trend (the niche researcher found no overpacker or suitcase-ride trend): the trend value sits in the music, the shared moves and the post text, and the client should be told so plainly. All four researchers worked from search summaries, not from the apps, so sounds, rules and charts must be checked in the live account on the day. pilot.title: One Night
pilot.hook_text: "When your friend packs for one night". Decision: YES, one line. Where: at the top of the frame, below the platform's top bar, in the series caption style (cream letters on the violet plate, sentence case, no full stop, no emoji), baked into the master so the same file goes to all three platforms. When: from frame one to 1.8 seconds; it is gone before Timo's caption appears at 2.0, so there are never two texts at once. Why: most people start with the sound off, and this line gives them the one fact the picture cannot show ('one night') in the words of a meme they already know. It is the first recommendation of the formats research and the most direct answer to 'what works on TikTok', and the brief allows one line. It is not needed to follow the story: the giant suitcase, the pointing arm and the open mouth tell the same thing, Timo's caption repeats it two seconds later, and the silent gate is run with the line covered. If a test viewer calls it advert-like, take it off; nothing else changes.
pilot.retell: His friend brought a giant suitcase for one night, and pushing it up the hill was so slow that a cat overtook them, so they rode it down the other side to the stadium, shot past the cat, and he ended up hugging the suitcase.

shots.place: A small square outside a train station in the invented football town: a plain cream arch with a soft cream-and-teal train carriage standing behind it. Late afternoon, low golden sun from the left, cobbles, plain bunting overhead. Behind Timo a street climbs steeply; over its top stand four floodlight masts.
shots.seen: From the first frame a yellow suitcase as big as a washing machine stands in the middle of the picture. On the left stands Luna, short, in a coral football shirt, one hand flat on its lid, smiling proudly. On the right, close to the camera, stands Timo, tall, in a teal jacket, one thumb under the strap of a tiny backpack, his other arm stretched out and pointing up the steep street to four floodlight masts. Both wear the same teal-and-coral scarf. Timo's eyes travel from the bottom of the suitcase up to its top. He turns his face to Luna and speaks, and his pointing arm sinks while he speaks. Luna answers with a huge grin and pats the lid twice.
shots.heard: Timo (at 2.0 s): "Luna. It's one night!" Luna, delighted (at 3.5 s): "Yes! One night!" Natural sound: a last rattle of small wheels and one heavy bump on the first beat, the hum of the train, a crowd far away, two hollow pats on the lid at 4.0 and 4.5. Music: the tick-tock and shaker start on frame one with no intro; Timo's line sits over the tick-tock alone; Luna's log drum enters at 4.0 and its first two notes are her two pats.
shots.caption: Luna. It's one night! (2.0 to 3.5) then Yes! One night! (3.5 to 5.0). The hook line is at the top from 0 to 1.8 only.
shots.start_picture: Everything is already in place. The suitcase is parked in the middle with its wheels below the bottom edge. Luna on the left: one hand flat on the lid, a closed-mouth proud smile, eyes on Timo. Timo on the right, three-quarters to the camera: face already towards the suitcase, eyes on its lower edge, mouth closed; the arm without the watch stretched out and pointing up the street; the watch arm with its thumb under the backpack strap. The pointing hand and the four floodlight masts sit below the top sixth of the frame, which is plain sky and bunting (room for the hook line). No face in the caption band. The clip adds: his eyes climb, he speaks and the arm sinks; she answers and her hand lifts and lands twice. Plan B if her line lands on the wrong mouth: she answers with a closed-mouth "Mm-hm!" and the two pats, with no caption.

shots.place: A steep cobbled street between painted houses, seen from the side: it climbs from right to left. Same golden sun. A garden wall runs along the far side, its top higher than everyone's heads. Over the top of the street, the four floodlight masts, bigger now.
shots.who: Luna, Timo and the ginger cat
shots.seen: The yellow suitcase is stuck halfway up the steep street and hardly moves. We see the friends from the knees up. On the left, above the suitcase, Luna leans back as in a tug-of-war, both hands on its handle, cheeks puffed out. On the right, below it, Timo pushes with both hands and one shoulder, his cheek squashed flat against the yellow shell, his face towards us. On top of the wall behind them a fat ginger cat strolls up the hill. It passes Timo, passes the suitcase, passes Luna. Both friends' eyes follow the cat together; their heads do not move. Ahead of them the cat stops and looks back once. The friends' eyes leave the cat and find each other.

Music: the lazy log drum and the late cowbell carry the shot; Timo's tick-tock runs at double speed against the slow wheels and falls back to normal when the cat looks round; at 8.0 it thins to bass and shaker.
shots.caption: none
shots.start_picture: Side view, the street climbing from right to left, friends from the knees up so that feet and wheels are out of frame. Both are already in held strain poses: Luna faces the suitcase and leans back with both hands on the front handle, cheeks puffed, eyes up at the wall; Timo has both hands and one shoulder on the shell, his cheek already flat on it, face to the camera, eyes up at the wall. The wall is on the far side with its top above all heads; the cat is already on it, in mid-stride, above Timo. shots.place: The top of the hill, same golden sun. On the far side the street falls away, long and straight, with roofs stepping down, to the stadium below: a round cream bowl with four lit floodlight masts and flags, bright in the sun, with small still shapes of fans around it.

On the left the suitcase stands on the last flat stones before the slope, and Luna is already sitting on the front half of its lid, turned towards Timo, feet off the ground, with a huge grin. One of her arms points straight down the hill at the stadium. She says two words to him. On the right Timo stands with both palms up and says no. shots.start_picture: The cat alone, sitting on top of the wall in the upper half of the frame, facing us, eyes half closed; the lower half is only the wall and the street. The clip adds: a gust from the right flattens its ears and fur, its head whips to the left, its eyes go huge. Still camera, one animal, no people. The streak is made in the edit, not generated: an approved side-view still of both friends on the suitcase, all four arms up, slides from right to left across the lower half with a soft smear and never overlaps the cat.

shots.place: The open space in front of the stadium, low golden sun from the left. Behind the friends the entrance is a bright warm glow under flags, with a few still, soft shapes of fans holding scarves up. At the left edge, soft, a small striped hut with shelves of bags.
shots.seen: Two clips of one idea. First, framed like the first shot: Luna on the left, the yellow suitcase in the middle, Timo on the right, with the glowing stadium entrance behind them. The suitcase stands still and a last puff of dust drifts away from its wheels. Timo is on his knees with his chest against the suitcase and both arms spread wide along its lid. He looks up, beaming, and speaks. Then he lays his cheek on the lid and closes his eyes, smiling. Luna leans on the lid from her side, laughing into her folded arms so that only her crescent eyes show. Second, closer: Timo's cheek on the yellow lid, eyes shut, smiling; Luna above him, her mouth hidden behind her arm, her free hand on his flat-top. She pats his head twice and says something, her shoulders shaking. Timo's eyes snap open and look straight into the camera. He does not let go of the suitcase. Luna laughs.
shots.heard: Timo (at 20.7 s): "I love this suitcase." A happy sigh. Two soft pats (23.0 and 23.5). Luna, laughing (at 23.8 s): "Timo. This is the small one." Then a full second of Luna's big laugh, not cut clean, running on under the card. Natural sound: the stadium roar swelling. Music: the hook returns on the downbeat at 20.5 with a warm round organ note; it drops low under both lines so that the last line stands alone.
shots.caption: I love this suitcase. (20.7 to 22.5) then, alone, after it has gone: Timo. This is the small one. (23.8 to 25.8)
shots.start_picture: 7a (2.5 s): framed like shot 1, camera low so that the lid sits a little above the middle and both faces are above the caption band. The hug is already in place: Timo on his knees, chest against the shell, arms spread along the lid with his hands on the two near corners, head up, beaming. Luna leans on the lid with folded arms, mouth hidden in them, crescent eyes on Timo. Behind them: the entrance glow, flags, still soft fan shapes, the bag hut soft at the left edge. The clip adds: his line, then his cheek goes down and his eyes close. 7b (3.5 s): the same side, closer. Timo's cheek is already on the lid, face to the camera, eyes closed, smiling. Luna's forearm lies on the lid with her chin and mouth tucked behind it; her other hand already rests flat on top of his flat-top. The clip adds: her hand lifts and lands twice; his eyes open wide into the lens. Her line is laid in the edit and needs no lips. Plan B: she pats the lid beside his head instead; if his eyes fail, hold the closed-eyes hug, which is complete without the reaction.

pilot.end_card: Two seconds (26.5 to 28.5) on the plain warm cream card: the word VENUVOY in deep violet in the middle, the teal-and-coral trip scarf lying flat under it like an underline, and two small words below: "football trips". Sound: Luna's laugh tails off under the first beat, then the last three claps of the theme on the last three beats, the final one dry. No logo animation, no app, no link, no slogan. The card cuts straight back to frame one, where the bump of the suitcase is beat one again, so the film loops. Shots 26.5 seconds plus card: 28.5 seconds.

interactions: THE PAT-PAT (Luna's invitation). Two flat-hand pats in the beat on whatever she is offering: her suitcase ('this one'), the empty seat beside her ('sit here') and, only when he is down at her height, Timo's flat-top ('well done'). Drawn in 3 seconds: her hand is already flat on the surface in the start picture and only lifts and lands twice. In the pilot it appears three times, and the third one is the touch between them.

'TRUST ME.' / 'NO. NO, NO, NO.' (the catchphrase pair and the sound the series owns). The one who offers says 'Trust me.' with a big gesture; the other holds both palms up, shakes the head and takes one step back. Always the same rhythm: 'No.' on one, two pats on two and three, 'no, no, no' on four, then a beat of nothing and the hard cut. Whichever friend says which half. Drawn in 3 seconds: the palms are already up in the start picture.

THE DOUBLE V (the picture after every 'No' cut). Luna in front, Timo behind and above her, both with both arms up in the same wide V, landing on the 'oh-oh-oh'. A short V inside a tall V reads at thumbnail size and with the sound off, and it says that the one who refused has joined in. Drawn in 3 seconds: the arms are already up in the start picture and only pump twice. It can be done standing anywhere, so viewers can copy it with a friend. A quiet bonus the film never points at: the brand's name has two V's.

THE FIVE-CLAP (the handshake, with no hands touching). Each claps their own hands over the head: clap, clap, clap-clap-clap. Timo is exact, Luna is a hair late, the last clap lands together and the hands stay open in the Double V. Hands and faces only, about two seconds, at most once per film, never a dance. Being a little out of step is in character, so a generated clip does not need perfect sync. In the pilot their hands are busy riding, so the five claps are in the music and the raised arms pump on them; the full version with hands starts in the second film.

THE NAME WITH A FULL STOP. They say each other's name as a whole sentence before the line: 'Luna. It's one night!' and 'Timo. This is the small one.' A film opens with one name and closes with the other, which tells a cold viewer both names without a label. Drawn in 3 seconds: one face turns to the other, one beat, then the line.

THE YES-ECHO (Luna's teasing). She answers his worry by repeating it as good news with 'Yes!' in front: 'It's one night!' / 'Yes! One night!'; 'It's raining!' / 'Yes! It's raining!'. Her word is Yes, his word is No, and after the cut he shouts her word. Drawn in 3 seconds: his worried eyebrows, then her grin.

FOUR EYES. Both pairs of eyes follow the same thing together with the heads perfectly still (the cat, a tray of food, a falling streamer), then the eyes leave it and find each other. No words. Drawn in 3 seconds, and it is the safest shared move for generated video because only eyes move.

THE YELLOW BUMP (who was right). After the payoff the one who said 'No' holds out a fist first and the other bumps it, over the big object of the film: teal cuff, coral cuff, yellow in between. Drawn in 3 seconds: the two fists already touch in the start picture and only push once. Fists, not hugs: friends, never a couple. It is not in the pilot, where the head pat does this job.

HALVES. Whatever Luna eats, half is Timo's. She holds one piece under his nose; the hand-over is always a cut: she has one, cut, he has one too, and they chew in the same rhythm. Drawn in 3 seconds as two matching pictures.

THE LOOK AT US. Once per film and never more, one of them looks straight into the camera for a second, as if at the third friend who is filming: always the one who has just been proved wrong. In the pilot it is Timo's eyes snapping open on 'the small one'. Drawn in 3 seconds: closed eyes, open eyes.

music.direction: KEEP THE THEME AND HARDEN IT. 'Tick Tock Clap' stays: sunny afro house with an amapiano log-drum bounce at exactly 120 beats a minute; Timo is the tick-tock on the beat, Luna is the lazy log drum with the late cowbell, and when they agree both lock under the five-clap and a rough three-note 'oh-oh-oh'. WHY IT READS AS CURRENT: the sound research describes this autumn's feed as club music with a bounce, bright, 120 to 135 beats a minute, led by drums and bass with tiny chopped vocal hooks, and reports afro house as the sound of 2026; comedy sketches run on their own audio, not on a song. So the genre was already right. What was missing are this year's markers: the groove starts in the first half second, the log drum has a mid-range knock that survives a phone speaker, a pitched one-syllable vocal chop answers the claps, an organ stab pumps with the kick, the claps are real hands in a dry room, the drop is set up by a dead stop and not by a riser, and the ending is abrupt and dry. The second lesson of the research: this year's biggest songs on the platform are old ones, so 'trendy' also means 'you can hum it after one viewing'. The test: play the pilot once and ask ten minutes later for the hook; if the viewer cannot hum or clap it, make it simpler. WHAT 'TRENDY' CANNOT MEAN: this month's hit. The sentence for the founder: 'Trendy means it sounds like this month's feed; it cannot be this month's hit, because labels are suing brands for exactly that, and a sound we own is the one that can become our trend.' HOW TO CHOOSE: generate brief A and the challenger brief B (64 seconds each, four variations, vocals allowed, never an artist or song name in the prompt), listen on a phone speaker at half volume with three people aged 18 to 25, pick one, then lock ONE master for the whole series, split it into stems and never generate the music again for a later film. Brief C is the loud option and the riskiest: it sounds like one country and can turn aggressive. If the model invents words, give it lyrics of only 'Oh, oh, oh', or make the chant and the claps as a separate stem in the same key and tempo. LIMITS: the genre evidence comes from search summaries of third-party trackers and reports, and genre fashion moves, which is why we pick a groove and not a gimmick.

briefs.name: A. Tick Tock Clap (keeps the bible; recommended)
briefs.style_prompt: Sunny afro house club track with an amapiano log-drum bounce. Exactly 120 BPM, 4/4, F major. No intro: on beat one a woodblock and muted marimba tick-tock, dead on the beat, with a tight shaker. After 8 seconds a lazy, knocky log-drum bass joins, with a mid-range knock that carries on a phone speaker, and a cowbell landing a little late. After 16 seconds it thins to bass and shaker, then one beat of total silence. Then the drop: soft four-on-the-floor kick, congas, off-beat open hi-hat, warm organ stabs pumping with the kick, a pitched-up one-syllable vocal chop every second bar, room handclaps playing clap, clap, clap-clap-clap, and four young friends singing a rough, slightly flat three-note oh-oh-oh, no words. Short shaker breakdown, groove returns, ends on three dry claps. Dry, close, hand-played. No guitar, piano, ukulele, whistling, risers, cinematic drums.

briefs.name: B. Sunny 2-Step (the challenger; the most 2026 for UK and European feeds)
briefs.style_prompt: Sunny, cheeky UK garage club track with a speed-garage bounce. Exactly 130 BPM, 4/4, G major. No intro: on beat one a woodblock tick-tock on the beat with shuffled closed hi-hats. After 7 seconds a swung 2-step drum pattern joins (kick on one, a late skipping kick, crisp rimshot on two and four) with a warm, round, bouncy organ bass riff that is clear on a phone speaker, bright filtered chord stabs and chopped, pitched-up one-syllable vocal slices used as rhythm. After 15 seconds it thins to bass and hats, then one beat of total silence. Then the drop: full 2-step groove, deeper bass, room handclaps playing clap, clap, clap-clap-clap, and four young friends singing a rough three-note oh-oh-oh, no words. Short breakdown, groove returns, ends on three dry claps. Dry, punchy, swung, warm. No MC, rap, sirens, air horn, dark bass, wobble bass, piano chords, risers.

briefs.name: C. Matchday Drums (the loud option; highest risk)
briefs.style_prompt: Bright daylight street-drum club track in a Brazilian funk rhythm, like a small drum corps outside a stadium. Exactly 130 BPM, 4/4, major key. No intro: on beat one a woodblock tick-tock and a tamborim pattern. After 7 seconds the funk hand-drum rhythm joins on real drums: low surdo, pandeiro, agogo bells landing a little late, a short punchy kick and a two-note bounce bass that carries on a phone speaker, with staccato one-syllable shout hits used as rhythm. After 15 seconds it thins to bass and shaker, then one beat of total silence. Then the drop: the full drum corps, handclaps playing clap, clap, clap-clap-clap, and a few young friends singing a rough three-note oh-oh-oh, no words. Short shaker breakdown, groove returns, ends on three dry claps. Playful, warm. No words in any language, no distorted cowbell melody, no dark or aggressive mood, no sirens, whistles, risers.

music.edit_plan: At 120 beats a minute one beat is half a second. Only three points must be exact: the drop, the entry of the voices and the claps on the card. Speech is never squeezed to fit the grid: move the music edit, not the mouth. Laughs and breaths stay loose. SHOT 1 (0.0 to 5.0, ten beats): beat one is the heavy bump of the suitcase. Tick-tock and shaker only for two bars. The hook line leaves at 1.8. Timo speaks at 2.0, on the bar line, over the tick-tock alone. At 4.0 Luna's log drum enters, and its first two notes are her two pats on the lid (4.0 and 4.5). SHOT 2 (5.0 to 8.5, seven beats): log drum and late cowbell. The grinding wheels run in time like a second shaker, the puffing falls on beats, the cat's 'mrrp' sits in a gap. Timo's tick-tock runs at double speed and snaps back when the cat looks round (leave this out if it sounds busy on a phone). At 8.0, as the friends' eyes meet, the music thins to bass and shaker. SHOT 3 (8.5 to 12.5, eight beats): bass and shaker under 'Trust me.' At 10.0 everything drops to the tick-tock alone: 'No.' on one, the two pats on two and three (10.5 and 11.0), 'no, no, no' at 11.5, 11.75 and 12.0. At 12.0 the tick-tock stops too, so the last 'no' lands on dead air, followed by about a quarter of a second of outdoor air and one wheel squeak. The six bars of build end here. THE CUT (12.5): the bar count starts again. SHOT 4 (12.5 to 14.5, one bar): the full groove lands on the first frame, and Timo's scream starts on that frame in place of a crash. SHOT 5 (14.5 to 17.5, six beats): the 'oh-oh-oh' and the five claps enter on the downbeat at 14.5, the scream becomes 'Yes!' on the same beat, and the raised arms pump on the claps. SHOT 6 (17.5 to 20.5, six beats): the music drops to shaker and tick-tock so that the gust, the two voices shouting 'Byeee!' and the small 'mrrow' (at about 19.8) are the joke. SHOT 7 (20.5 to 26.5, three bars): the hook returns on the downbeat at 20.5 with a warm round organ note under it. The music is lowered 6 to 9 dB under 'I love this suitcase.' The cut to the closer picture is at 23.0, and the two head pats are on the beat at 23.0 and 23.5. Under 'Timo. This is the small one.' only the tick-tock and the organ stay. His eyes open on the beat at about 25.5, and Luna's laugh fills the last second. CARD (26.5 to 28.5, one bar): one beat of breath with the tail of the laugh, then three claps at 27.0, 27.5 and 28.0, the last one dry. The cut back to frame one at 28.5 is beat one again, and the bump of the suitcase answers the three claps. THE SAME SEVEN SECONDS IN EVERY FILM: from 'Trust me.' to the first laugh after the drop, the music, the rhythm of the 'No' and the length of the silence never change. IF BRIEF B OR C WINS (130 beats a minute): keep the beat counts per shot (10, 7, 8, 4, 6, 6, 12); the shots then run about 24.5 seconds, the card needs five beats (2.3 seconds), and shot 7 gets two more beats if its lines feel hurried. MIX: natural sound as loud as the music; start at about -14 LUFS with peaks under -1 dBTP (not an official platform figure) and judge in mono on a phone speaker at half volume, where the log drum must still be heard as a knock. Any music or voices that the video clips made by themselves are removed. No library meme effects.
music.platform_sound_plan: THE RULE (from the sound and niche research, read from search summaries and vendor sources and not from the platforms' own help pages; this is not legal advice). A brand account cannot put a trending commercial song under its video on TikTok, Reels or Shorts. A sped-up version, a remix, a cover, 'only five seconds', a credit in the caption or posting from a personal account changes nothing; several brands were sued for this in 2025 and 2026. WHAT WE DO. (1) Our own theme is mixed into the film file, and the same master goes to all three platforms on the same day. On TikTok the upload becomes an 'original sound' under the account. (2) If the app shows the 'Music Usage Confirmation' box, tick it, and keep the proof that we hold the rights: the prompt, the date, the job number and the paid-plan receipt of the music generator, whose terms must allow commercial use. (3) Before the pilot goes out, make one private test upload from the real account with the real master, to see what the app asks and whether other people can reuse our sound (the sources disagree). (4) After posting, rename the sound 'Trust me. No, no, no. (Plan, No Plan)' so that it can be found. Never delete a posted film, because that can kill its sound; set it to private if needed. Never ask viewers to 'use this sound'. (5) Before release, run the master through a song-recognition app, which must find nothing, and ask two football fans whether the hook reminds them of a real chant. HOW THE CLIENT STILL RIDES TRENDS LEGALLY. By sounding like this month's feed (genre, tempo, vocal chop). By using the formats of current trends with our own audio (see the trend formats). And, only if he wants a library sound, by choosing a track marked as approved for business use in TikTok's Commercial Music Library for a TikTok-only extra such as a loop: never for the main cut, because it would replace our theme and break the beat-synced edit, and never cross-posted, because that licence covers TikTok only. On Instagram the equivalent is Meta's royalty-free Sound Collection; on Shorts only music we own or have licensed. NOT DONE. Another account's 'original sound' that contains music; the hidden-sound trick (a trending sound at 1 to 3 percent volume); an AI vocal that imitates a real voice; a hook that echoes a real chant. If he ever wants a real hit, the only route is a paid licence for the song and for the recording. Rules and menus change, so confirm them in the live account in the week of posting.

trend_formats.name: The 'No' cut with the drop (the refusal smash cut)
trend_formats.how: A friend offers, the other refuses, and one hard cut later both are doing it; the music stops for a beat on the 'No' and the full beat lands on the cut. It is a timeless comedy device, not a November trend (the formats researcher found no named trend), and a cut on the drop is still the basic TikTok edit. We own it by keeping the same seven seconds in every film: 'Trust me.' / 'No. No, no, no.' / silence / drop / a scream that turns into a laugh, published as a named original sound that other people can film their own version to.
trend_formats.episode_idea: Try It: Timo wants to eat the neat sandwiches he packed, Luna holds a huge steaming flatbread under his nose and says 'Trust me', he says no, and one cut later he has a flatbread in each hand and sauce on his chin while she happily eats his sandwiches.
trend_formats.shelf_life: Evergreen. Our own sound gets stronger with every film that repeats it.

trend_formats.name: Two friends, two types, one frame (the planner and the one who just shows up)
trend_formats.how: The standing travel meme: one picture shows two opposite travellers side by side, and the viewer picks a side in the first second and says which one they are in the comments. The series already is this meme. So every film has one side-by-side frame that reads at thumbnail size (his small neat thing next to her big thing), a one-line 'When your friend ...' hook where it helps, and the same question in the post text: 'Plan or No Plan: which one are you?'. The labels 'Type A / Type B' and 'round or square' are never said or shown: they must be read and they already have a backlash.
trend_formats.episode_idea: Just In Case: under a blue sky Timo packs two rain ponchos into his tiny backpack and Luna laughs, points at the sun and says no; one cut later a sun-shower pours, both are dancing to the stadium in ponchos, and she hugs his tiny backpack.
trend_formats.shelf_life: Evergreen as a picture, but crowded (hotels and airlines have used it since 2025), so it needs our characters to stand out. The label words last weeks.

trend_formats.name: The slow friend and the waiting friend (the situation under the 'Go go go' trend)
trend_formats.how: One friend takes her time and the other stays very polite while his patience runs out; this month it circulates with a 'go, go, go' voiceover. We borrow only the situation, with no trend audio and no voiceover. The impatience is played by Timo's tick-tock running at double speed and by one small movement (his watch hand tapping), while Luna does not hurry at all.
trend_formats.episode_idea: Hello, Cat: Timo marches towards the floodlights but Luna has stopped to stroke the cat; he refuses to stop, and one cut later he is sitting on the cobbles with the cat asleep on his lap, not daring to move, while Luna is the one pointing at the stadium.
trend_formats.shelf_life: The audio trend: weeks, and we do not use it. The situation: evergreen.

trend_formats.name: Solo, solo, together (the shape of this month's duo dances)
trend_formats.how: The biggest two-person format this week is a short routine in which each does a solo and both lock together at the end. The named dances were already falling on 13 November on one third-party chart and their sounds are not cleared, so we take only the shape, which is already our music: Timo's tick on the beat, Luna a little late, both together on the five-clap, hands open into the Double V. Upper body only, about two seconds, once per film, never a dance.
trend_formats.episode_idea: The Clap: outside the gate Luna joins the home fans' clap loudly and wrongly while Timo knows it but claps tiny and shy; a local fan offers to show her, she says no, and one cut later he is teaching her clap by clap until all three clap over their heads together.
trend_formats.shelf_life: The named dances: weeks (do not copy them). The shape and our own five-clap: evergreen.

trend_formats.name: Hold one thing back until the last second
trend_formats.how: Travel accounts that keep the answer for the final seconds were measured at several times their usual reach this month (one vendor, a small sample). Each film keeps its best line or picture for the last second before the card and never gives it away in the post text. Across the series one question stays open, 'What is in Big Yellow?'. Each time the suitcase opens (always as a cut: closed, then already open) it gives one new thing and never everything, so no film needs an earlier one.
trend_formats.episode_idea: Three Hours Early: Timo's plan gets them to the ground first and there is nowhere to sit; Luna pats Big Yellow, he says no, he will stand, and one cut later both are in beach chairs under a sunshade from the suitcase, with the cat asleep in the open lid.
trend_formats.shelf_life: Evergreen. The suitcase question needs a small answer every few films, or it turns into a gag that depends on earlier films.

trend_formats.name: Same morning, two ways (parallel cutting, from 'How Different Our Lives Are')
trend_formats.how: A late-summer format: the same day of two friends, cut back and forth, showing how differently they live it. The named trend is two to three months old and its sound is a commercial recording we cannot use, so we never call it 'the trend'. We use it as plain parallel cutting: full-frame shots of about two seconds each, no split screen, no labels, his tick-tock under his shots, her log drum under hers, and both together on the last shot. It needs about six start pictures, so it costs nearly as much as an episode.
trend_formats.episode_idea: Same Morning: on the morning of the trip Timo is dressed, knotted and first at the empty station while Luna sleeps and then runs with toast in her mouth, and they still put their hands on Big Yellow at the same second and do the five-clap.
trend_formats.shelf_life: The named trend peaked in August and September and is late. Parallel cutting itself is evergreen.

trend_formats.name: The reaction close-up loop
trend_formats.how: A still face that holds one clear feeling for a few seconds; people reuse such a clip as their own reaction. Between films we post new edits of six to eight seconds (new cuts, never reposts) built on a reaction that survives a square crop: Timo's cheek squashed on the yellow shell with only his eyes moving, or the cat with its fur blown flat. If a line is put on it, the line is about the situation and never about Timo being slow.
trend_formats.episode_idea: Faster Than You: two friends push a giant suitcase uphill so slowly that a cat strolls past them, and one cut later they shoot past the same cat downhill and its fur blows flat.
trend_formats.shelf_life: The named 'silent face' trend: weeks. Reaction clips and an unimpressed cat: evergreen.

trend_formats.name: Two pictures, one swap on the beat (the structure of 'Shoulder Carry')
trend_formats.how: A trend made of two still pictures and one swap exactly on a sound cue. The trend itself is falling, is tagged as a couples trend and needs a song we cannot use, so we keep only the structure: two designed start pictures, no video generation, the swap on the first clap of our theme. It is the cheapest thing we can post, and it is the 'No' cut in its smallest form.
trend_formats.episode_idea: No Scarf: Timo holds both palms up to the smiling scarf seller because today's rule is no shopping, and on the clap he stands in three scarves, a hat and a flag as a cape, prouder than anyone, while the seller waves.
trend_formats.shelf_life: The named trend: over within weeks. The two-picture swap: evergreen, best as a teaser between films.

posting_kit.caption: One night. One suitcase this big. Plan or No Plan: which one are you?
posting_kit.comment_prompt: Pinned first comment from the account, one line: "What is in Big Yellow?" The either-or question (Plan or No Plan: which one are you?) is already in the caption, so the comments get a second, different thing to answer. Never write 'tag a friend', 'share' or 'comment below'.
posting_kit.cover_text: "Luna. It's one night!" The cover is the frame at about 2.5 seconds: the hook line has gone, Big Yellow fills the middle, Luna is on the left, Timo on the right with his mouth open, and the film's own first caption sits on its plate. No extra title layer and no second typeface. If a platform asks for typed cover text, use the title: One Night.
notes: AI label: switch it on at upload on TikTok, Reels and Shorts, for the pilot and for every cut-down. Account line: 'Two best friends. Football trips abroad. Animated with AI, written and directed by people.' Claim only the human work that is true.
Same master, same day, on all three platforms, with our own theme mixed in. Never add an in-app sound to the main cut, and never cross-post a TikTok export that carries a library track.
Before the pilot: one private test upload from the real account with the real master, to see what the app asks about the music and whether other people can reuse the sound.
After posting: rename the original sound 'Trust me. No, no, no. (Plan, No Plan)'. Never delete a posted film (set it to private if needed). Do not ask viewers to use the sound.
Naming: on Shorts the title is 'Plan, No Plan: One Night'. Make a playlist called 'Plan, No Plan' on TikTok and on Shorts. No numbers, no 'Part', no 'previously'.
Launch burst: have three finished films before the pilot is posted and release them inside the first ten days, so a viewer who likes one film is served the next.

Comments: answer early comments as Team Plan or Team No Plan. Keep two replies ready. For the scarf: 'Yes, it is a half-and-half scarf. Half him, half her.' For AI: 'Yes, it is AI animation. The story, the designs and the song are ours.' Do not delete or argue with 'AI slop' comments. Save 'Name the cat.' for the second film.
Words: plain sentences only. No slang, no 'POV', no 'Type A / Type B'. Never put the last line of the film ('the small one') in the caption or in a comment: it is the reveal.

Hashtags: the same five in the same order on every post, so the series can be found as a set. No tournament, league or club tag, never 'soccer'. The list is the researcher's judgement; no view counts were found for these tags.
Extras for the first two weeks, each a new edit and not a repost: the cat loop 'Faster Than You' and one two-picture teaser.

Checks on the day (the research came from search summaries, not from the apps, and none of it is legal advice): TikTok's Creative Center and each platform's help pages for the music and AI-label rules; the hook line and captions clear of the top bar, the right-hand buttons and the bottom text on a real phone; the receipts for the music kept in one place.
Before any of this: version 3 must pass the strip gate and the silent gate again (muted, with the hook line and all captions covered). The 9 out of 10 belongs to version 2.

What to tell the client in one sentence: the story is an evergreen situation and not a trend; the trend value sits in the music that sounds like this month's feed, in the moves the two friends share, and in the post text.

retell: Two mates get off a train in a football town for a match. Luna, the short one, has brought a yellow suitcase the size of a washing machine. Timo, the tall one, only has a tiny backpack and tells her it's one night. They heave the thing up a steep street while a fat cat strolls past them. At the top the stadium is straight down the hill. Luna sits on the case and says "Trust me", Timo says no four times, and then it cuts to both of them riding it downhill, him screaming and then loving it. They blast past the cat and stop in front of the stadium. Timo hugs the case and says he loves it, and Luna tells him it's her small one. Then a card: Venuvoy, football trips.
who_wants_what: Timo wants to get to the ground with no fuss: he packs light, he's the sensible one, and he does not want to ride a suitcase down a hill. Luna wants to bring everything she owns and turn the walk into a laugh, and she wants Timo to go along with it. She wins and he ends up more into it than she is. Neither of them seems to want anything to do with the match itself: nobody is late, nobody mentions the game.
best_moment: The cut after "No, no, no": a tiny beat of silence, one wheel squeak, then straight into Timo mid-scream on the suitcase with the beat dropping. That is the one moment I'd actually laugh out loud, and it is the bit I'd rewatch on the loop. Second best is Timo's eyes snapping open and looking into the camera at the end without letting go of the case.
confused: Why are they dragging the suitcase to the stadium at all? Anyone who goes to away games knows you would never get that through a turnstile, so I kept waiting for a steward or a bag check and it never came. I half saw a little hut with bags at the edge of the last shot but could not tell if that was meant to be the answer.
What Venuvoy actually is. 'Football trips' could be an agency, an app, packages or a ticket site. The card told me nothing about what they would do for me.
'This is the small one': I got it after a beat (there is an even bigger one somewhere), but it landed softer than the downhill cut, so the film peaks in the middle and the end is just a smile.
'One night' comes at me three times in five seconds (top line, Timo's caption, Luna's caption). Not confusing, but I noticed I was being told the joke before I'd looked at the picture.
No idea whether they are in a hurry. There is no kick-off time or clock, so the uphill push is just effort with nothing riding on it.
the_two_friends: They work as a pair straight away: she's chaos, he's the careful one who caves. The small things feel like real mates: both sets of eyes following the cat and then finding each other, her twisting round to look at him on the way down, her patting his head at the end. The talking is what doesn't. They say each other's names every time ("Luna. It's one night!", "Timo. This is the small one."), in clean, complete sentences with no swearing and no taking the piss, which is how characters in a kids' show introduce themselves, not how my mates talk on a matchday. I like them, I don't quite believe them. I would tag someone, but because of the premise, not the characters: I have a mate who brings a full case for one night in Dortmund, and the top line is basically his name.
feels_current: Half and half, and it leans towards a very well made brand cartoon rather than something from my feed. What feels current: the "When your friend packs for one night" line, starting on the gag with no intro, the "Trust me / No" hard cut into the scream, the look to camera, the loop, and the log-drum groove (fine, though that sound is not exactly new any more). What gives it away as an advert: everything is spotless and sunny, the two wear matching scarves in what are obviously brand colours, the "oh-oh-oh" with claps sounds like a jingle and then comes back on the logo card, and nothing in it is specific enough to football to have come from a fan. What gives it away as a kids' show: toy figures in a model town, a cat as the third character, both shouting "Byeee!", and the name-first dialogue. It did not make me swipe, because there is no logo until the very end and the first frame is already the joke, but I knew by about the cat that someone was selling me something.
one_change: Make it about a football trip instead of about a suitcase. Right now this could be an ad for luggage or a city break, and the stadium is just scenery. Give me one thing only someone who travels to matches would recognise, ideally as the ending: the moment at the gate where that case obviously is not getting in, or the two of them racing kick-off. "This is the small one" is fine, but it is a joke anyone could write. A matchday truth is what would make me think this was made by people who actually go, and that is what would get it sent to my away-days group chat.

retell: Two friends come out of a train station in a football town. The short girl, Luna, has a yellow suitcase as big as a washing machine and is very proud of it. The tall boy, Timo, has only a tiny backpack and tells her it is only one night. She says yes, one night, and pats the suitcase. They push and pull it up a very steep street and it hardly moves; a fat ginger cat walks past them on a wall, easily, and looks back at them. At the top they see the stadium far down a long straight street. Luna sits on the suitcase, points down and says "Trust me." Timo says no, no, no and steps back. Cut: both are riding the suitcase down the hill, Luna with her arms up, Timo screaming and holding her shoulders. Then Timo is laughing too, with his arms up like hers. They shoot past the cat and the wind blows its fur. At the stadium Timo is on his knees hugging the suitcase and says "I love this suitcase." Luna laughs, pats his head and says "Timo. This is the small one." His eyes open and he looks at the camera. Then a cream card: VENUVOY, a scarf, "football trips".
who_wants_what: Both want to get from the train to the stadium for the match. Luna wants to bring her giant suitcase and sees no problem with it; later she wants Timo to trust her and ride it down the hill. Timo wants to travel light and thinks the suitcase is crazy for one night; he does not want to ride it, but after the ride he loves it and does not want to let go. The cat wants nothing; it is just faster than them, then gets a shock. At the end I understand that the film wants me to know Venuvoy does football trips.
best_moment: The hard cut from the caption "No. No, no, no." straight to Timo's screaming face in the gap above Luna's head while she has both arms up. I saw it coming and still laughed. With no sound it works completely, because his face is the joke. Second best is Timo's eyes snapping open and looking into the camera after "This is the small one."
confused: The line at the top went away too fast for me. It is seven words and gone in under two seconds, while I am also looking at the giant suitcase and two people. I read about half. I only got 'one night' for sure from Timo's caption after it.
In the last close-up Luna's mouth is hidden behind her arm. With no sound I could not see who was talking. I knew it was her only because the caption starts with 'Timo.' It took me a moment.

In the first shot Timo points at something up the street. I did not see what, because I was reading and looking at the suitcase. I understood where they were going only at the top of the hill, when the stadium is below them.
The small striped hut with shelves of bags at the edge of the last shot. If it is a place to leave bags, is that part of the joke? I was not sure if I missed something.

VENUVOY: I understand 'football trips', but not what it is exactly (an app, a travel company, do they book the train and the ticket?). Nothing in the story shows what they do for me, and I am not sure how to say the name.

I cannot say anything about the music or the claps. With the sound off they do not exist for me. In the downhill shots the two shout something as they pass the cat, I think, but there is no caption. I did not need it.
the_two_friends: Yes, they feel like friends, not like two mascots. I get who is who after five seconds: she is the bold, chaotic one who is proud of her bad idea, and he is the careful one who says no and then has the most fun. The parts that sell it are small: both pairs of eyes following the cat and then finding each other, his arms going up in the same V as hers, her patting his head at the end. I would tag someone, because everyone has a friend who packs like this, and the first frame plus "It's one night!" is enough to write "this is you". One honest limit: it is a pair I have seen before (small crazy one, tall nervous one) and they are very sweet to each other. Real friends tease a bit harder. The last line is the only moment where she really gets him.
feels_current: In between. It feels like a good brand cartoon made for TikTok, not like something a person posted. What feels like now: the "When your friend..." line at the top, the cut straight from "No, no, no" to them doing it, the look into the camera at the end, that it is short and loops. I cannot judge the music at all with the sound off; the film works without it.
one_change: Leave the line at the top on screen longer, at least until the end of the first shot. I did not finish reading it in 1.8 seconds, and on TikTok this kind of text normally stays up, so it would also look more like a real TikTok. Two texts on screen for a moment is normal for me there.
